sections.title: Flexible cords and cables — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 400 covers flexible cords and flexible cables — the connections between equipment and the building wiring, not wire that is installed as part of the building. It sorts cord types by construction (Table 400.4) and permitted use, and it draws a hard line against using a cord as a substitute for permanent wiring. If the wire is meant to stay in the building, it belongs in a Chapter 3 wiring method, not in a cord.
Uses permitted (400.10) are the ones that need to move or be serviced:
• Pendants
• Portable lamps and portable appliances
• Elevator and hoist cables
• Parts of listed equipment, and similar flexible connections
Uses not permitted (400.12) — a flexible cord may not be:
• (1) Used as a substitute for the fixed wiring of a structure
• (2) Run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors
• (3) Run through doorways, windows, or similar openings
• (4) Attached to building surfaces, except as 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit
• (5) Concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings
• (6) Installed in raceways, except as otherwise permitted in the Code
• (7) Installed where subject to physical damage
The 2020 numbers are 400.10 and 400.12; in the 2017 book the same lists were 400.7 and 400.8.
sections.on_the_job: When you reach for a cord, ask whether the equipment is meant to move, be serviced, or be exchanged. If the answer is no, run a permanent wiring method instead. On a service call at a small Orlando warehouse, Sharma found an air compressor 'temporarily' cord-connected through a hole bored in the wall for over a year, the cord pinched flat where it crossed a doorway. The fix was not a heavier cord: the crew ran a dedicated 20 A branch circuit in EMT to a receptacle beside the compressor — Sharma's commercial minimum — and the cord went back to being the compressor's own short connection. Check the cord jacket marking for the type letter before you trust it in a damp or hard-use location.
sections.why_it_exists: A cord jacket is not a raceway. Building wire gets mechanical protection, support, and a box at every splice; a cord pressed into permanent service gets none of that. Stapled, buried, or pinched in a doorway, its insulation fails quietly — and nobody re-checks it, because everyone assumes the 'temporary' cord was removed years ago.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'use a heavier cord.' A 12 AWG hard-service cord through a wall hole is still a 400.12(2) violation, and an extension cord feeding a fixed appliance is still a substitute for fixed wiring under 400.12(1). Cord size and jacket type never cure a prohibited use.
inspection_fails: Flexible cord run through a hole in a wall, ceiling, or floor to reach fixed equipment (400.12(2)).
Cord passing through a doorway or window opening, pinched by the door (400.12(3)).
Extension cord or cord set left as the permanent supply to a fixed appliance (400.12(1)).
Cord concealed above a suspended ceiling, or attached to building surfaces outside the permitted exceptions (400.12(4), (5)).

sections.title: Uses permitted and not permitted — flexible cords (400.10 / 400.12)
sections.plain_explanation:
Sections 400.10 (uses permitted) and 400.12 (uses not permitted) draw the line for flexible cords; 400.7 and 400.8 are the 2017 numbers. Permitted uses are the ones that need to move or be serviced: pendants, portable lamps and appliances, elevator and hoist cables, parts of listed equipment, and similar flexible connections. The not-permitted list is the one that fails inspections: a cord may not substitute for the fixed wiring of a building, run through holes in walls, ceilings, or floors, pass through doorways or windows, attach to building surfaces outside the narrow exceptions, hide inside walls or conduit, or sit where it will be damaged. If a cord is doing a cable's job permanently, it is the wrong wiring method.
The 400.12 list, in Code order — flexible cords may not be:
• (1) As a substitute for the fixed wiring of a structure
• (2) Run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors
• (3) Run through doorways, windows, or similar openings
• (4) Attached to building surfaces (except as 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit)
• (5) Concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings
• (6) Installed in raceways, except as otherwise permitted in the Code
• (7) Installed where subject to physical damage
sections.on_the_job: Service call in a Winter Park home: a chest freezer in the garage is fed by a cord that passes through a hole drilled in the wall from the laundry room, and the garage door closes on it. It has been 'temporary' for two years. The fix is not a heavier cord — it is a real receptacle on its own 20 A circuit where the freezer stands, and the cord run comes out. The same answer applies to the window air conditioner found on the next call, running on a cord pinched under a bedroom door.
sections.figure_idea: Two-column card: 'cord is fine here' scenes (pendant, portable tool) versus 'hardwire it' scenes (through a wall, under a door).
sections.why_it_exists: A flexible cord has no armor and no raceway around it. Run through a wall or under a door, it gets pinched, abraded, and cooked out of sight, and nobody sees the damage until it faults or starts a fire. Fixed wiring methods are built to live inside a building for decades; a cord is built to flex, be inspected at a glance, and be replaced. The two lists keep each method doing its own job.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that 400.12 bans cords attached to building surfaces, period. Two exceptions exist — 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit attachment in their cases. The reverse trap also shows up: a cord inside a raceway is not automatically fine; 400.12(6) allows it only where the Code otherwise permits.

Cord passing through a doorway and pinched by the door — 400.12(3).
Extension cord stapled along a baseboard as permanent wiring — 400.12(1) and (4).
Cord hidden above a dropped ceiling feeding a sign — 400.12(5).

sections.title: What flexible cords may be used for
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 400.10 lists the jobs a flexible cord is allowed to do: hanging fixtures, connecting portable equipment, appliances that need to be moved for cleaning or service, and similar uses where flexibility is the point. The common thread is that the equipment, not the building, is what moves. A cord feeding a fixed outlet box or a permanent load is outside this list.
Cord ampacity comes from Table 400.5(A)(1) for the cord type and the number of current-carrying conductors — the table below gives the sizes a crew actually holds, figured for two current-carrying conductors. A third current-carrying conductor in the same cord drops the value (the table's next column), which is why a cord's rating is read off its own table and not off the building-wire ampacity table.
sections.on_the_job:
Before you plug or hard-wire a cord to anything, name the 400.10 use out loud. If you cannot name one, stop and run conduit or cable. Watch especially for cords run through walls, ceilings, or doorways, which this article does not allow.

Workshop rough-in: pendant drops over the benches are a listed use, and the portable saw connects the same way. When the owner later asks for a cord through the wall to feed a new fixed outlet, that is the stop point — the use is gone, so the cord goes.
sections.why_it_exists: A cord is built to flex, not to live inside a wall for thirty years. Its insulation and strands are lighter than building wire, and nothing protects it where it passes through framing or gets pinched in a door. Kept to the listed uses, a cord stays out in the open where damage shows. Buried as permanent wiring, it becomes the hidden weak link that overheats or shorts.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating a heavy cord like building wire: '12 AWG is 12 AWG.' A cord's ampacity comes from Table 400.5(A)(1), not Table 310.16, and no cord size buys a use that is not on the 400.10 list. A cord feeding a fixed outlet box fails on the use before size is even discussed.
inspection_fails: Flexible cord run through a wall, ceiling or doorway to reach a fixed load.
Cord used as a substitute for fixed wiring — feeding an outlet box or a permanent appliance.
Cord ampacity taken from Table 310.16 instead of Table 400.5(A)(1).
Three current-carrying conductors in the cord, but the two-conductor ampacity used.

sections.title: Uses not permitted — flexible cords and cables
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 400.12 is the stop list for flexible cords and cables. In the 2017 edition this list was numbered 400.8; the 2020 reorganization of Article 400 moved it here. Unless 400.10 permits the use, a flexible cord, flexible cable, cord set, or power-supply cord may not be used:
• (1) As a substitute for the fixed wiring of the structure.
• (2) Run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors.
• (3) Run through doorways, windows, or similar openings.
• (4) Attached to building surfaces — except that cords used for temporary wiring under 590.4 may be attached.
• (5) Concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings — except within an enclosure for use in other spaces used for environmental air, as permitted by 300.22(C)(3).
• (6) Installed in raceways — except as 400.17 permits in industrial establishments where only qualified persons service the installation.
• (7) Where it is subject to physical damage.
Most failed cord installations fail here, not on ampacity: the cord is usually heavy enough — it is just doing a job the Code reserves for fixed wiring.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call, trace the whole cord, not just the ends. If any part of it is stapled, hidden, or passing through a partition, the fix is a permanent wiring method, not a heavier cord. A Marion Oaks garage call: a freezer in the corner runs on a 14 AWG cord stapled along the wall and passed through a hole into the house — three items on the stop list at once. The fix was a new 20 A circuit in 12 AWG to a receptacle at the freezer, not a 12 AWG cord. And when a plan shows a cord doing a building's job, price the Chapter 3 wiring method instead.

sections.why_it_exists: A cord is built to flex, not to live inside a wall for thirty years. Hidden or pinched, its jacket dries, cracks, and chafes where nobody can see it, and it has no raceway or cable armor to protect it. The stop list keeps cords out in the open, where damage shows, and reserves hidden runs for wiring methods built to be buried.
inspection_fails: Extension cord stapled along a garage wall feeding a freezer — a substitute for fixed wiring, 400.12(1) and (4).
Cord run through a hole in the wall between the house and the garage, 400.12(2).
Appliance cord pinched through a doorway that closes on it, 400.12(3) and (7).
Cord draped above a dropped ceiling to feed a projector, 400.12(5).
Cord pulled into a raceway on a commercial job outside the 400.17 industrial exception, 400.12(6).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer treats the stop list as an ampacity problem: 'use a heavier cord and it passes.' It does not. A 10 AWG cord run through a wall still violates (2), and a cord stapled to the wall still violates (4), whatever its size. The only cure for a 400.12 violation is a fixed wiring method — or a use that 400.10 actually permits.

sections.title: Fixture wires — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 402 covers the small conductors used inside fixtures and equipment, called fixture wires. They are for wiring within a luminaire or similar equipment and for connecting that equipment over a limited distance, not for general branch-circuit runs through a building. Sizes run smaller than branch wiring, which is exactly why they must stay inside the equipment they belong to.
• Uses permitted (402.10): inside luminaires and similar equipment, enclosed or protected and not subject to bending or twisting in use, and for connecting luminaires to the branch-circuit conductors that supply them.
• Uses not permitted (402.12): fixture wires are not branch-circuit conductors, except where another article permits them, such as Class 1 remote-control and signaling circuits.
• The smallest size is 18 AWG (402.6), and ampacity comes from Table 402.5, not Table 310.16: 18 AWG is 6 A and 16 AWG is 8 A, whatever the insulation type.
• Protection is by the tap rules (240.5(B)(2)): on a 20 A circuit, an 18 AWG tap may run 50 ft and a 16 AWG tap 100 ft.
sections.on_the_job: If you find a fixture wire run acting like a branch circuit through a wall or ceiling, flag it. Replace that run with a Chapter 3 method sized for the circuit. Keep fixture-wire splices inside the fixture or its listed outlet box. On a high-bay retrofit the pattern is: 12 AWG branch wiring to the box on the 20 A circuit, then the fixture's own 18 AWG whip down to the luminaire. A 25 ft tap is inside the 50 ft limit, and the LED driver draws about 1.5 A against the whip's 6 A ampacity. The wire between two fixtures is not a tap: it is branch wiring, and it stays Chapter 3 wire.
sections.why_it_exists: Fixture wire ratings are figured for the inside of a fixture: short runs, known loads, and the fixture's own heat. Run it through a building like branch wire and a 6 A conductor can end up sitting on a 20 A breaker with nothing to save it. The tap limits in 240.5 are the compromise: short, load-limited whips are fine; a building run is not.
inspection_fails: Fixture wire run through a wall or ceiling as a branch circuit.
18 AWG fixture wire tap over 50 ft long on a 20 A circuit.
Fixture wire spliced in the open, outside the fixture or its listed box.
Fixture wire loaded past its Table 402.5 ampacity.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for Table 310.16, or for the small-conductor rules, to rate fixture wire. Fixture wire has its own table: 18 AWG is 6 A, not 15 A. The 20 A breaker is allowed behind it only because 240.5(B)(2) treats the whip as a tap with a length limit, not because the wire carries 20 A.

sections.title: Fixture wire ampacity — small wire, small numbers (Table 402.5)
sections.plain_explanation:
Fixture wires are the small conductors inside luminaires and equipment, and Table 402.5 gives them their own ampacities — not the branch-circuit numbers for the same gauge. The whole table is five rows:
• 18 AWG fixture wire — 6 A
• 16 AWG fixture wire — 8 A
• 14 AWG fixture wire — 17 A
• 12 AWG fixture wire — 23 A
• 10 AWG fixture wire — 28 A
Fixture wire is protected and tapped under the fixture-wire rules (240.5), never treated as branch-circuit wire, and it never leaves the fixture or equipment it belongs to. No fixture wire is smaller than 18 AWG (402.6).
sections.on_the_job: Rewiring a fixture whip or a driver lead: match the fixture wire to what the fixture came with. Never extend a circuit with fixture wire because it was handy on the truck. A 16 AWG whip is an 8 A conductor — plenty for an LED driver lead, nowhere near a circuit. Where fixture wire taps a 20 A branch circuit, 240.5(B)(2) caps the run: 18 AWG up to 50 ft, 16 AWG up to 100 ft, and 14 AWG or larger without the length cap.
sections.figure_idea: Gauge ladder: 18 AWG to 6 A, 16 AWG to 8 A, with a red line where branch-circuit wire tables take over.

sections.why_it_exists: Fixture wire runs inside a hot, closed metal box, bundled against ballasts and drivers, in sizes too small to survive a hard fault on a big breaker. Its own ampacity table, and the tap limits in 240.5, keep a fault inside the fixture from turning the whip into a heating element. Extend a run with it, or load it to branch-circuit numbers, and the weak link is hidden where nobody will see it smoke.

The exam names the conductor — fixture wire gets the fixture table. The dangerous reverse is loading a branch circuit to the 23 A fixture number.

sections.title: Switches — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 404 covers switches: the devices that open and close a circuit, from a simple single-pole snap switch to motor-circuit switches. It handles which conductor a switch may interrupt, where a grounded (neutral) conductor must be available at a switch box, how high and how accessible a switch must be, and how switch terminals are marked for conductor materials. The working rules:
• Switching belongs in the ungrounded (hot) conductor — a switch never interrupts the neutral alone (404.2(A)).
• A grounded conductor (neutral) must be present at most switch locations, so electronic controls, timers and sensors can power themselves (404.2(C)). Listed exceptions exist — raceways where the neutral can be pulled in later, certain replacements — so read the exception list for the exact job.
• Switches must be readily accessible, and the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or platform (404.8(A)). That is a ceiling, not a mounting height.
Start here whenever a switching question is about the device itself rather than the circuit feeding it.
sections.on_the_job: On rough-in, the two 404 questions to settle before the walls close are neutral availability at switch boxes and switch height. Both are cheap at rough-in and expensive after drywall. Sharma sets switches at 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent (S-05) — a company preference, not a code number; the code only caps the operating handle at 6 ft 7 in. (404.8(A)). Pull the neutral through every switch box on the rough, even where today's device is a plain snap switch: the dimmer or occupancy sensor that replaces it later will need it.
sections.sharma_note: S-05: when the plan is silent, Sharma sets switches at 48 in. to the center of the box. That is a company preference, not an Article 404 requirement.

nec2023_change.change: The switch article's scope now makes clear that wireless controls with no connection to circuit conductors aren't covered, and an informational note sends readers to 210.70. sections.why_it_exists: A switch is the one part of the circuit a person touches every day, often in the dark, sometimes with wet hands. Switching the hot conductor means the load is dead when the switch is off; switching the neutral leaves the fixture live and waiting. The neutral in the box exists because a generation of dimmers, timers and sensors was stranded in boxes with no way to power itself, and the height ceiling keeps a switch or disconnect within reach of a person standing on the floor.

No grounded conductor in the switch box, and no 404.2(C) exception applies.
Operating handle center over 6 ft 7 in. in its highest position (404.8(A)).
Snap switch loaded past its limit for the load type — motor load over 80 percent of rating (404.14).

Under 404.2(C) the grounded conductor belongs in the box unless a listed exception fits the job — a box roughed in without it fails the next device change.

sections.title: Three-way and four-way switching — what the switch may control
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.2(A) is about which conductor a switch interrupts. For three-way and four-way switches the rule is stated outright: all switching must be in the ungrounded (hot) conductor.
• The grounded (neutral) conductor is never switched. It runs unbroken to the load and lands on the screw shell of a lampholder, so the shell — the part fingers touch — stays on the grounded side.
• In a traveler system, the hot lands on the first switch's common terminal, the two travelers carry it from switch to switch, and the switched leg leaves the last switch's common for the load. Two or more locations control one load while the rule stays intact.
• The banned pattern is the old Carter system: hot and neutral both landed on the traveler terminals, so depending on the switch positions the shell could sit on the hot side — with the light off. Prohibited since the 1923 NEC, it still turns up in old Florida houses.
sections.on_the_job: Wire 3-way/4-way runs by function, not by color habit: common, travelers, switched leg, neutral, ground. On a Sharma house rough-in — a Winter Park two-story with switches at both ends of the hall and at the top and bottom of the stairs — the travelers on the long runs get labeled at rough-in, per the Sharma practice note below, so the trim crew is not ringing out pairs through finished walls. Test every switch position at trim and confirm the load is fully controlled from each location before you leave. Never borrow a neutral from another circuit to make a traveler scheme work.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice note (job practice, not code text): label travelers at rough-in when a run is long or passes through several boxes. It saves the trim crew from ringing out pairs.
sections.figure_idea: Figure idea (original, ours): a simple line drawing in our own style showing one load, a 3-way at each end and a 4-way in the middle, with boxes labelled common / travelers / switched leg — no textbook diagram copied.
sections.why_it_exists: A lamp that is 'off' should be safe to re-lamp. If the switching scheme leaves the screw shell connected to a hot conductor, the person changing the bulb — standing on a ladder, one hand on the shell — becomes the path. Switching only the hot conductor, and keeping the shell on the grounded conductor, is what makes 'off' mean off.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is wiring by 'it works.' A Carter-wired 3-way turns the light on and off from both locations, so it passes a lazy test — but in some switch combinations the socket shell is hot with the light off. 'The light works from both switches' is not the test; 'all switching is in the ungrounded conductor' is. The same goes for landing a traveler on the common because the colors looked right.
inspection_fails: Neutral switched instead of the hot — the lampholder shell stays energized with the light off (404.2(A)).
Carter-style wiring found or recreated: hot and neutral both on the traveler terminals.
Traveler landed on a common terminal, so the load obeys only one switch or the positions disagree.
Neutral borrowed from another circuit to make a traveler scheme work.

sections.title: A neutral must be available at most switch locations
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.2(C) requires a grounded conductor — the neutral — to be installed at the switch locations where switches control lighting loads on a grounded general-purpose branch circuit: bathrooms, hallways, stairways, and habitable rooms. The reason is practical: modern controls, timers, occupancy sensors and smart switches need a neutral to power themselves.
• The neutral must be there even if today's device is a plain snap switch that never touches it.
• Where 3-way or 4-way locations control the same load and the whole floor area is visible from the switch locations, the neutral is required at only one location.
• Exceptions (2020) let you omit it where the conductors enter through a raceway with room to add the neutral later, where a cable can still be added or replaced without removing finish materials, for snap switches with integral enclosures complying with 300.15(E), where the lighting is controlled by automatic means, and where the switch controls a receptacle load.
Read the exception list for the exact job instead of assuming — and pull the neutral anyway when in doubt.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, pull the neutral through every switch box even when the planned device is a plain snap switch that does not use it today. Cap it neatly in the back of the box. That one habit prevents the most common 404.2(C) correction and makes later smart-switch work possible without opening walls. On a Marion Oaks entry, the 3-gang box gets the feed, three switch legs, and the neutral spliced through and capped; the hall 3-ways need the neutral at one location only, because the whole hall is visible from both ends.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: this is why the Honeywell / ecobee-era control work and smart switches on Sharma jobs assume a neutral in the box. Do not design a switch location that strands a future electronic control without one.

nec2023_change.change: One escape hatch for skipping the neutral at lighting switches is gone: a box you can get into later without opening up the finish no longer counts. Gone in 2023: the pass for a switch box reachable later without removing finish materials. Pull the neutral anyway (404.2(C)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 404.2 Neutral at switch locations

sections.why_it_exists: Electronic controls need power while the light is off. Without a neutral in the box, the old workarounds leaked current through the load or borrowed the equipment ground — flickering lamps and current on grounding paths. Requiring the neutral at rough-in, while the walls are open, turns every later control swap into a device change instead of a demolition job.
inspection_fails: Switch loop roughed with no neutral in a bedroom or hallway switch box.
Smart dimmer landed on the equipment grounding conductor for its return current.
Neutral present in the box, but from a different circuit than the switch leg it serves.
No neutral at any 3-way location where the room is not visible from the switch locations.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'no neutral needed — the specified device is a plain snap switch.' The rule is about the location, not today's device: if the switch controls lighting in a habitable room, the neutral goes in the box. The related trap is powering a smart switch by borrowing the equipment grounding conductor as its return — electronic control switches are not permitted to put their operating current on the ground (404.22).

sections.title: Switches in damp or wet locations — and out of the tub/shower wet location
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 404 requires switches installed in damp or wet locations to be in enclosures suited to the location, and it separately restricts switches in a bathtub or shower space:
• A switch may not be installed within the wet location of a tub or shower unless it is part of a listed tub or shower assembly made for that purpose.
• The rule parallels the receptacle and luminaire zones in 406.9(C) and 410.10(D) — measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold — so the wettest part of the room is kept free of devices a wet person would operate.
• A switch on the dry wall outside that space is an ordinary installation.
sections.on_the_job: At layout, treat the tub/shower wet location as a no-switch zone the same way you treat it as a no-receptacle zone: in a Florida master bath, the switch bank goes on the dry wall outside the 3 ft / 8 ft zone, not on the wall beside the tub where the sketch first puts it. Exterior and patio switches get weatherproof enclosures suited to whether a cover must close over a plug or cord. Pool and spa switching also answers to Article 680 — check Chapter 6 before you place a switch near water.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: outdoor kitchens, lanais, and pool-adjacent switching are damp or wet locations in practice; enclosure choice matters more here than the switch itself.
sections.why_it_exists: Water on skin drops the body's resistance, and a person in a tub is usually wet, barefoot, and in contact with grounded plumbing — the worst possible position to touch a line-voltage device. Keeping switches out of the wet location removes the device from the reach of the person least able to survive contact with it. The weatherproof enclosure rule does the quieter job outdoors: it keeps water out of the device so the device does not fail wet.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that GFCI protection makes a switch legal inside the tub/shower wet location. It does not — this is a location rule, and the only way in is as part of a listed tub or shower assembly. The second trap is treating a damp-location cover as a wet-location installation. A wet location needs an enclosure suited to wet use, not just a gasketed plate over an indoor switch.

sections.title: Switches must be reachable — operating handle height
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.8(A) requires switches to be readily accessible and sets a ceiling on height: the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or working platform. The point is that a person standing on the floor must be able to operate the switch without a ladder or a reach tool. It does not set the normal mounting height for a house switch — that comes from the plan or company practice.
• The measurement is to the center of the handle with the handle up — not to the top of the box or the plate.
• Special cases exist for switches next to the equipment they serve and for busway-type installations, so check the exceptions before you relocate a switch that looks too high.
sections.on_the_job: Sharma roughs house switches at 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent (S-05), so the ceiling in 404.8(A) rarely comes up — until it does. On an Ocala final, the garage switch for the yard lights had been set high to clear a workbench: the center of the handle in the up position measured 6 ft 8 in. One inch over the limit, and it failed. It moved down to 5 ft 6 in., still clear of the bench.
sections.sharma_note: S-05: Sharma's default is 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent. The plan governs when it states a height. Do not present 48 in. as a code number — 404.8(A) is the code ceiling, S-05 is our working height.
sections.why_it_exists: A switch is the control a person reaches for in the dark, in smoke, or in a hurry. If it takes a ladder or a broom handle, it is not really a control — people leave the light on, or worse, cannot shut a circuit off at the device. The 6 ft 7 in. ceiling keeps every switch within a standing person's reach.
inspection_fails: Switch handle center at 6 ft 9 in. above the floor — over the 404.8(A) ceiling.
Switch reachable only from a step stool or ladder in a garage or stairwell.
Switch blocked by fixed equipment or stored material — not readily accessible.
Height checked to the top of the plate at trim and a high switch passed on that measurement.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering 48 in. That is Sharma's working height (S-05), not a code number. The code gives a maximum, not a mounting height: 6 ft 7 in. to the center of the operating handle in its highest position. The second trap is measuring to the top of the box — the rule measures the handle.

sections.title: Grounding snap switches (404.9)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.9 requires snap switches — including dimmers and control switches — to be connected to an equipment grounding conductor (EGC), so the metal yoke and any metal faceplate are bonded.
• Metal box: the box is bonded by its EGC, and the switch's mounting screws bond the yoke to the box (250.109). The screws are the bond — use the switch's own mounting screws, tight.
• Nonmetallic box: there is no box to bond through, so the EGC lands on the switch's own green grounding terminal.
• Faceplates: 404.9(A) also requires the plate to completely cover the box opening and seat against the finished surface.
The replacement exception matters in old houses. Where an existing switch is replaced in a box with no grounding means — no EGC in the wiring method — an ungrounded replacement is permitted for replacement only, on the exception's terms: a nonmetallic, noncombustible faceplate with nonmetallic screws, or GFCI protection for the circuit. Where the switch sits within 8 ft vertically or 5 ft horizontally of ground or exposed grounded metal objects, those terms are the whole allowance. Landing a standard switch with a metal plate on a 2-wire box and moving on is not one of the paths.
sections.on_the_job: On remodels, check for a ground before trim-out, not during the final walk. In a 1960s Orlando ranch wired with 2-wire cable, Sharma's crew found no EGC in any switch box on the lighting circuits. Because the panel was being replaced with new Siemens gear anyway, the fix was GFCI breakers on those lighting circuits, which puts every replacement switch on the exception's GFCI path; on the one circuit that stayed unprotected, the plates went on nonmetallic, with nonmetallic screws. No EGC in the box changes what devices you may land — flag it at discovery.
sections.figure_idea: Yoke-to-box bond sketch: EGC to a metal box with the switch screws bonding the yoke; green terminal to EGC in a plastic box.
sections.why_it_exists: The yoke and the plate screws sit right where fingers land in the dark. If a hot conductor faults to an unbonded yoke, the plate and its screws sit at line voltage with nothing to trip the breaker, and the first person to touch the switch becomes the fault path. The EGC gives that fault a low-impedance road home, so the breaker opens instead.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'The switch is in a metal box, so it is grounded.' A metal box is a grounding path only when the box itself is connected to an EGC. A steel box fed by old 2-wire cable bonds the yoke to a floating box — worse than plastic if the box ever faults. The second trap: GFCI protection does not create a ground. It is the exception's alternative protection for a replacement, not an equipment ground.

Ground wire clipped off or left loose in a nonmetallic box instead of landed on the switch's green terminal.

sections.title: Snap switch ratings and the loads they may control
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.14 ties a general-use snap switch to the kind of load it controls. A switch marked for AC only, or for AC/DC, has different limits for motor, inductive, and tungsten-type loads, and a switch may not be loaded past the rating that applies to that load type. In plain terms: the amp number on the yoke is not a promise for every load — the load type decides which limit applies.

The working limits, by load type:
• Resistive loads — up to the switch's full marked ampere rating
• Inductive loads (ballasts, transformers) — full rating on an AC general-use switch; 50 percent of the rating on an AC/DC general-use switch
• Motor loads — 80 percent of the rating on an AC general-use switch, or the switch's marked horsepower rating where it has one
• Tungsten-filament lamp loads — full rating at 120V on an AC general-use snap switch (404.14(A)); the 'T' rating question applies to AC/DC switches (404.14(B))
Worked example: a 15A AC-only snap switch may carry a 12A motor load (15 × 0.80) and up to 15A of tungsten lighting at 120V; the 'T' marking question applies to AC/DC switches.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma commercial service call in Orlando, a 15 A AC-only snap switch controls a small exhaust fan motor that draws 12 A. The check before touching it: motor loads are limited to 80 percent of the switch rating, and 15 × 0.80 = 12 A, so this switch is right at its limit and legal. The same switch on a 14 A motor would be over the limit — that one gets a switch with a marked horsepower rating, or the motor gets controlled through a rated contactor. Read the yoke marking before any snap switch goes on a motor, a ballast bank, or a heater, and run the percentage for that load type.

nec2023_change.change: Switch terminals now have wire rules: copper or copper-clad aluminum unless CO/ALR, and push-in holes are for 14 AWG solid copper, only on 15-amp circuits. Dimmers now follow the same load rule as timers. Push-in (back-stab) holes take only 14 AWG solid copper on a 15-amp circuit, unless the switch is listed and marked for other wire (404.14(D)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 404.14 Switch terminals and dimmer loads

sections.why_it_exists: A snap switch's contacts are small. Motor and inductive loads draw inrush current and throw an arc every time the switch opens, and cold tungsten filaments pull many times their running current at switch-on. Load a switch past the limit for that load type and the contacts pit, weld shut, or cook inside the box — you get a motor that will not turn off, or a switch that heats every time it is used. The load-type limits keep the contacts alive for the life of the switch.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating the yoke number as universal: '15 A switch, 15 A load, done.' A 15 A AC/DC switch on an inductive load is limited to 50 percent — 7.5 A — and a 15 A AC switch on a motor load tops out at 12 A. The load type picks the limit, not the number stamped on the yoke.
inspection_fails: 15 A snap switch switching a 14 A motor load — over the 80 percent motor limit of 404.14.
AC/DC-rated switch loaded to its full ampere rating on a fluorescent ballast bank.
General-use snap switch with no horsepower rating used to control a motor beyond its rating.
Switch controlling a heater bank loaded past its marked ampere rating.

tables.caption: 404.14 load limits for a general-use snap switch
rows: Up to the switch's full marked ampere rating
Full rating on an AC switch; 50% of rating on an AC/DC switch
80% of rating on an AC switch, or the switch's marked horsepower rating
Full rating at 120 V on an AC switch (404.14(A)); the T-rating question applies to AC/DC switches (404.14(B))

figures.alt: Bar chart of what a 15 ampere general-use snap switch may carry by load type: resistive 15 A, inductive 15 A on an AC switch and 7.5 A on an AC/DC switch, motor 12 A, and tungsten 15 A at 120 volts on an AC switch.
figures.caption: Same 15 A switch, four different limits — the load type decides.

page_quiz.question: A 20 A AC general-use snap switch controls a motor load. What is the maximum motor load?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Motor loads are limited to 80 percent of the switch rating: 20 × 0.80 = 16 A, unless the switch carries a horsepower rating for the load.

page_quiz.question: An AC/DC general-use switch rated 15 A feeds an inductive load. What is its limit?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Inductive loads on an AC/DC general-use switch are limited to 50 percent of the rating: 15 × 0.50 = 7.5 A.

page_quiz.question: What does an AC/DC switch need before it may control a tungsten-filament lamp load?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The T-rating question applies to AC/DC switches under 404.14(B); AC snap switches carry tungsten loads at full rating at 120 V under 404.14(A).

sections.title: Switch terminal markings for conductor materials (CO/ALR)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 404.15(C) carries the CO/ALR marking rule for switches — the switch-side twin of 406.3(C) for receptacles:
• A switch designed for the direct connection of aluminum conductors must be marked CO/ALR.
• The terminal rules that go with the marking, stated for the 2020 NEC in NEMA Engineering Bulletin No. 122 from the UL guide information for snap switches: terminals of 15A and 20A snap switches are for use with copper and copper-clad aluminum conductors only, unless marked CO/ALR, which adds aluminum.
• Terminals of switches rated 30A and above are for copper only, unless marked AL/CU.
• Plain aluminum never lands on an unmarked device terminal.
sections.on_the_job: On a service call in a 1970s Florida house with aluminum branch wiring, the replacement switch on the truck is not automatically the right device. Read the terminal marking on the switch you are holding and match it to the conductor you are landing: no CO/ALR marking, no plain aluminum on the terminal — get a CO/ALR device instead of landing it and leaving. With CCA the terminal itself is fine, but land it on the screw terminals only: do not backstab CCA (see S-10).
sections.sharma_note: S-10 applies: CCA is sized one AWG larger than copper and terminations must be listed for the conductor. Never backstab.
sections.why_it_exists: Aluminum and copper do not age the same way under a screw. Aluminum oxidizes and creeps under pressure, so a terminal that was not designed and tested for it can work loose over years of heating and cooling until the connection runs hot. A CO/ALR device is built and tested for that behavior. The marking is how the installer knows which test the terminal passed — from the outside, the two switches look the same.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that CO/ALR and AL/CU are two names for the same marking. They are not: 15A and 20A snap switches take aluminum only when marked CO/ALR, while switches rated 30A and above are copper only unless marked AL/CU. The second trap is treating CCA as plain aluminum. The bulletin puts copper-clad aluminum with copper on an unmarked 15A or 20A terminal; plain aluminum is the conductor that needs the marking.

tables.caption: What may land on the terminal (NEMA Engineering Bulletin No. 122, for the 2020 NEC)

figures.alt: Three panels comparing switch terminal markings: an unmarked 15 or 20 amp snap switch takes copper and copper-clad aluminum only; a CO/ALR marked switch also takes aluminum; a switch rated 30 amps and above is copper only unless marked AL/CU.
figures.caption: Read the device mark before you land the wire.

page_quiz.question: A 15 A snap switch has no CO/ALR marking. Which conductors may land on its terminals?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Per NEMA Bulletin No. 122, 15A and 20A snap switch terminals are for copper and copper-clad aluminum unless marked CO/ALR, which adds aluminum.

page_quiz.question: A switch rated 30 A must land aluminum conductors. What marking is required?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Switches rated 30A and above are for copper only unless marked AL/CU.

The print on the wire insulation
page_quiz.explain_plain: The terminal marking is on the device: CO/ALR on a 15A or 20A snap switch, AL/CU at 30A and above.

sections.title: Receptacles, cord connectors, and attachment plugs — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 406 covers receptacle outlets and the plugs and cord connectors that go into them: how receptacles are rated and grounded, when a replacement must upgrade protection, where face-up devices may be used, what damp and wet locations demand, the tub and shower exclusion zone, and where tamper-resistant receptacles are required. It is the article behind most device-level corrections on a residential final.
• Ratings, grounding and replacements (406.4): receptacles match the circuit's rating and configuration, are grounding type where the wiring method provides a ground, and a replacement follows the 406.4(D) upgrade ladder, including GFCI protection and 'No Equipment Ground' marking where no grounding means exists.
• Damp and wet locations (406.9): weather-resistant receptacles and the covers the location demands.
• Tub and shower zone (406.9(C)): no receptacles within a zone measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or shower stall threshold.
• Tamper-resistant (406.12): TR receptacles in dwelling units and the other listed occupancies, with exceptions such as receptacles more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor.
sections.on_the_job: At trim, work 406 as a checklist room by room: correct replacement type, WR where the location needs it, in-use cover where the location is wet, TR where 406.12 requires it, and nothing inside the tub/shower zone. The bathroom is where the zone bites: the basin receptacle has to sit within 3 ft of the basin (210.52(D)) and still stay out of the 3 ft by 8 ft zone measured from the tub rim, so measure from the rim, not from the basin, before the box is set.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: points marked GFI on a Sharma plan get a standard tamper-resistant receptacle protected by the dual-function breaker. Sharma does not install GFCI receptacles as the standard device.

nec2023_change.change: One section, 406.2, now holds the no-reconditioning rule for receptacles, cord connectors, plugs and flanged surface devices. The ban itself dates to 2020. None of these four can be reconditioned: receptacles, attachment plugs (caps), cord connectors and flanged surface inlets or outlets.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 406.2 Reconditioned receptacles and plugs

nec2023_change.change: 406.3(D) now spells out what wire receptacle terminals take: copper or copper-clad aluminum unless CO/ALR, and push-in holes are for 14 AWG solid copper, only on 15-amp circuits. Push-in (back-stab) holes are for 14 AWG solid copper only, on a 15-amp branch circuit, unless the receptacle is listed and marked for other wire.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 406.3 Receptacle terminal wire rules

nec2023_change.change: Cover plates with a night light or USB charger that draw power through spring contacts on the receptacle screws are now limited to 1 watt and brass or copper alloy screws. A plate whose only connection is spring-tensioned contacts touching the receptacle's terminal screws can't draw more than 1 watt (406.6(D)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 406.6 Night-light and USB cover plates

nec2023_change.change: The tub and shower zone now reaches inside and below the tub and gained new exceptions. Weather-resistant listing now covers 30-amp, 50-amp and other wet-location receptacles, and hinged hood covers must open 90 degrees. The zone now covers inside the tub or shower and everything below the rim; a wall, floor, door, window or fixed barrier ends it.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 406.9 Damp, wet and tub-zone receptacles

sections.why_it_exists: Receptacles are the part of the system people touch every day, often with wet hands, near water, or through a child with a paperclip. Article 406 is where the Code puts the device-level defenses: the right rating, a real ground, GFCI protection on replacements, weather resistance outside, shutters for kids, and a hard line keeping devices away from tubs and showers.
inspection_fails: Receptacle installed inside the tub and shower zone (406.9(C)).
Standard receptacle in a wet location: not weather-resistant, and no in-use cover.
Non-TR receptacle in a dwelling unit where 406.12 requires tamper-resistant receptacles.
Replacement receptacle swapped like-for-like where 406.4(D) requires GFCI protection and 'No Equipment Ground' marking.
Face-up receptacle in a countertop that is not listed for face-up use.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is mixing up the two 3 ft rules in a bathroom. The basin rule (210.52(D)) wants a receptacle within 3 ft of the basin; the zone rule (406.9(C)) bans receptacles within 3 ft horizontally of the tub rim. A receptacle can satisfy the basin and still fail the zone.

page_quiz.explain_plain: The zone is measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or shower stall threshold, and it includes the space directly over the tub or shower.

page_quiz.question: Which receptacle is excepted from the 406.12 tamper-resistant requirement?
choices: A receptacle more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor
page_quiz.explain_plain: Receptacles located more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor are one of the listed exceptions to 406.12.

page_quiz.question: A nongrounding receptacle is replaced where no grounding means exists. One permitted path is…

page_quiz.explain_plain: 406.4(D) permits a GFCI replacement marked 'No Equipment Ground' where no grounding means exists.

sections.title: Receptacle installation and replacement — the general rules (406.4(A)–(C))
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.4 sets the baseline before the replacement details in 406.4(D). Receptacles must be of the grounding type where the wiring method provides a ground, must match the circuit's rating and configuration, and replacements follow a ladder:
• Grounding-type for grounding-type where an EGC exists. Where an EGC exists or is connected under 250.130(C), the replacement is a grounding-type receptacle (406.4(D)(1)).
• Where no grounding means exists, the permitted paths are a nongrounding replacement, a GFCI replacement marked 'No Equipment Ground,' or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked the same way.
• The third replacement option is exactly this: a grounding-type receptacle supplied through a GFCI, marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground' (406.4(D)(2)(c)).
The markings are part of the rule, not paperwork.
sections.on_the_job: Old two-wire house work — a 1960s Orlando home with no EGC in the boxes: carry GFCI receptacles and 'No Equipment Ground' stickers on the truck. Where the owner wants a three-slot receptacle, the path is a GFCI replacement marked 'No Equipment Ground,' or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground.' An unmarked GFCI swap in a no-ground box fails the detail even though the device itself works.
sections.figure_idea: Three-rung ladder graphic for a no-ground box: nongrounding replacement, GFCI marked, grounding-type through GFCI marked.

nec2023_change.change: Food court and transit waiting-area floor receptacles now need GFCI, a CO/ALR replacement on aluminum wire can skip tamper-resistant, and a replacement must provide GFPE wherever GFPE is now required. GFCI now covers 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp floor receptacles in food courts and airport, bus and train waiting areas that allow food or drink (406.4(G)(2)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 406.4 Receptacle replacements and floor receptacles

sections.why_it_exists: A grounding-type receptacle on a circuit with no ground tells a lie to the next person who plugs in: the third slot promises a fault path that is not there. The replacement ladder keeps the protection honest. A GFCI gives real shock protection without pretending to be a ground, and the 'No Equipment Ground' marking tells the truth about what is actually in the box.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is the unmarked GFCI swap: 'the GFCI trips, so the replacement is legal.' The device working is not the rule — on a no-ground circuit the GFCI replacement must be marked 'No Equipment Ground,' and a grounding-type receptacle fed through one needs both markings. The second trap is a plain grounding-type receptacle on a two-wire circuit. Without the GFCI and the markings, the ground slot promises a ground that does not exist.

figures.alt: Flow chart for receptacle replacement: with an equipment grounding conductor in the box the replacement is a grounding-type receptacle; with no ground there are three permitted paths under 406.4(D)(2), each with its required marking.
figures.caption: The replacement ladder: ground in the box, or one of three marked paths.

inspection_fails: GFCI receptacle swapped into a no-ground box with no 'No Equipment Ground' marking.
Grounding-type receptacle on a two-wire circuit with no GFCI protection and no markings — a ground slot with no ground behind it.
Receptacle fed through a GFCI but missing its 'GFCI Protected' marking.
Replacement receptacle that does not match the circuit's rating or configuration.

page_quiz.question: No EGC exists in the box. Which replacement is permitted?
choices: A GFCI receptacle marked 'No Equipment Ground'
A grounding-type receptacle with the ground terminal jumpered to the neutral
page_quiz.explain_plain: With no grounding means, the paths are a nongrounding replacement, a marked GFCI replacement, or a grounding-type receptacle through a GFCI with both markings.

page_quiz.question: Where an EGC exists in the box, the replacement receptacle must be:
choices: Whatever was cheapest on the truck
page_quiz.explain_plain: 406.4(D)(1): where an EGC exists or is connected under 250.130(C), the replacement is a grounding-type receptacle.

page_quiz.question: A grounding-type receptacle supplied through a GFCI on a no-ground circuit must be marked:
choices: Nothing — the GFCI is the protection
page_quiz.explain_plain: 406.4(D)(2)(c) requires both markings on that replacement path.

sections.title: Replacing a receptacle — the replacement must meet today's rules for that location
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.4(D) sets the rules for swapping an existing receptacle. The replacement is not grandfathered: where today's code requires GFCI, AFCI, tamper-resistant, or weather-resistant protection at that location, the replacement must provide it.
• Ground in the box — 406.4(D)(1): if a grounding means exists in the enclosure, or an equipment grounding conductor is run under 250.130(C), the replacement must be a grounding-type receptacle, connected to that ground.
• No ground in the box — 406.4(D)(2): exactly three paths are permitted. (a) Another non-grounding-type receptacle. (b) A GFCI-type receptacle marked "No Equipment Ground." (c) A grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI, marked "GFCI Protected" and "No Equipment Ground."
• The protection family rides along: GFCI where required (D)(3), AFCI where 210.12 requires it (D)(4), tamper-resistant where 406.12 requires it (D)(5), weather-resistant where required (D)(6). An automatically controlled receptacle is replaced with an equivalently controlled one (D)(7).
A plain grounding receptacle on an ungrounded circuit, left unmarked, is never one of the paths.
sections.on_the_job: Service call in a 1962 Orlando ranch: the bathroom receptacle by the sink is dead, the box has no equipment ground, and the panel is an older one with no GFCI or AFCI protection at the breaker. Test first — no ground. The legal swap is a GFCI-type receptacle marked "No Equipment Ground," which also gives that location the GFCI protection today's code requires there. Apply the marking before you leave and photograph it for the job record. On Sharma's own newer work the picture flips: protection lives at the dual-function breaker (S-07), so a replacement on that circuit normally stays a standard tamper-resistant device.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 note: on new Sharma work the GFCI/AFCI protection lives at the DFN breaker, so a replacement on a Sharma DFN circuit normally keeps a standard TR device. On older panels without that protection, 406.4(D) is what forces the upgrade at the device.

nec2023_change.change: Substantiation was provided to that will require ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) receptacles to be listed per 406.4(D)(3).
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 406.4(0)(3) Ground-Fault Circuit-Interrupter Protection

nec2023_change.change: Substantiation has been provided to to require ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) to be provided for replacement receptacles that require GFPE protection by current Code requirements elsewhere in the NEC
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 406.4(0)(8) Ground-Fault Protection of Equipment (GFPE)

sections.why_it_exists: A replacement is the one moment an old installation gets touched, so the code uses it to close the gaps that hurt people: ground-fault protection where water is present, arc protection on bedroom circuits, shutters where children push objects into slots. The marking rules exist because a three-prong face on an ungrounded circuit lies to the next person. Plug-in testers, surge strips, and metal-cased tools all assume that ground pin is real.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "The old receptacle was three-prong, so a standard three-prong replacement is fine." If there is no equipment ground in the box, that device is not on the list. The permitted paths are a non-grounding replacement, a marked GFCI replacement, or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked. And a GFCI does not create a ground — it protects people, and the device has to say so.
inspection_fails: Standard grounding-type receptacle installed on an ungrounded circuit, unmarked — not a permitted 406.4(D)(2) path.
GFCI-type replacement in a no-ground box without the "No Equipment Ground" marking (406.4(D)(2)(b)).
Grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI but missing the "GFCI Protected" and "No Equipment Ground" markings (406.4(D)(2)(c)).
Replacement at a bath or kitchen location without the GFCI protection current code requires (406.4(D)(3)).
Neutral jumpered to the ground terminal — a bootleg ground — to make a tester read "grounded."

page_quiz.question: A receptacle box has no equipment grounding conductor. Which replacement is permitted?

A grounding-type receptacle with the neutral jumpered to the ground terminal

page_quiz.explain_plain: 406.4(D)(2) allows exactly three paths. The grounding-type one is (c), and both markings are required.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Replacements are not grandfathered: where GFCI protection is required elsewhere in the Code, the replacement receptacle must be GFCI protected.

page_quiz.question: A GFCI-type receptacle replaces a two-prong receptacle in a box with no ground. What marking is required?
choices: No marking — the GFCI creates a ground
page_quiz.explain_plain: The GFCI protects people from shock; it does not create an equipment ground, so the device must be marked "No Equipment Ground."

sections.title: Receptacle assemblies in countertops and work surfaces — listed for the surface
sections.plain_explanation:
A receptacle assembly installed in a countertop surface has to be listed for countertop applications — an ordinary receptacle in a cut-in box does not become countertop equipment by being set into the surface.
• Where the assembly is required to provide GFCI protection under 210.8, it is permitted to be a GFCI receptacle assembly listed for countertop applications.
• Section 406.5(F) applies the same listing rule to receptacle assemblies in work surfaces.
• Whether a receptacle may sit face-up in that surface at all is the next rule, 406.5(G): face-up is allowed only for assemblies listed for countertop or work surface use, and never in the area below a sink.
The listing is the point: a countertop assembly is tested for the spills, heat and cleaning that a countertop actually sees.
sections.on_the_job: On a Winter Park kitchen island, the plan shows one receptacle in the island top and one on the cabinet side. The one in the top goes on the material list as a listed pop-up countertop assembly — the GFCI version, because kitchen countertop receptacles need GFCI protection under 210.8. The side receptacle is an ordinary tamper-resistant duplex in the cabinet side; it is not in the surface, so 406.5(E) does not govern it. Do not let the counter fabricator cut a hole sized for a standard duplex in the stone.
sections.figure_idea: Section through a kitchen island: a listed pop-up countertop assembly with its listing tag called out, beside a standard duplex in a cut box with a red X.
sections.why_it_exists: A countertop is a wet work surface. Liquids spill, pots overflow, and crumbs and metal utensils sit on it all day. An ordinary receptacle face set into that surface collects whatever lands on it, straight into the slots. A listed countertop assembly is built and tested for that exposure — sealed, spill-shedding, and made to be cleaned.
inspection_fails: Standard duplex receptacle cut into a quartz island top.
Desk or grommet outlet assembly used in a kitchen counter — not listed for countertop applications.
Countertop assembly without GFCI protection where 210.8 requires it.
Face-up receptacle installed in the counter area below the sink.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'any receptacle can go in the countertop as long as it is GFCI protected.' GFCI protection and countertop listing are different requirements — the assembly must be listed for countertop applications. The reverse trap is 'face-up receptacles are banned everywhere': a listed countertop assembly may sit face-up, just never in the area below a sink.

A standard duplex if the breaker is GFCI

sections.title: Face-up receptacles in countertops — the prohibition is 406.5(G)
sections.plain_explanation:
406.5(G) carries the face-up rule for receptacles in countertops and work surfaces.
• (G)(1): a receptacle may not be installed in a face-up position in or on a countertop or work surface unless it is listed for countertop or work surface applications.
• (G)(2): a receptacle may not be installed face-up in the area below a sink at all — the listed-assembly exception does not apply there.
• The hazard is the position itself: a face-up device collects spills, crumbs and liquids directly into its face.
• The listing rule for the receptacle assemblies made for these surfaces is at 406.5(E) and (F), covered on the previous page.
sections.on_the_job: On a Marion Oaks kitchen, the island is 8 ft long with the sink at one end. The plan's island receptacle cannot be a standard duplex cut face-up into the stone — it is not listed for countertop use. The fixes: a listed pop-up assembly in the counter away from the sink, a receptacle on the side of the cabinet, or one on the wall at the backsplash. Nothing goes face-up in the area below the sink, listed or not.
sections.figure_idea: Countertop from above: a standard duplex crossed out face-up in the surface, a listed pop-up assembly beside it, and the zone below the sink marked no face-up.
sections.why_it_exists: A face-up receptacle is a shallow cup wired to power. Coffee, dishwater and cleaning spray fall straight into the slots, and crumbs and dropped utensils land across the contacts. Below a sink it is worse: a slow plumbing leak can drip into the device for weeks before anyone opens the cabinet and notices. The listing requirement, and the flat ban below a sink, keep liquid and debris out of live parts.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is 'listed means anywhere.' A listed pop-up assembly is legal face-up in the counter under (G)(1), but (G)(2) bans every face-up receptacle in the area below a sink — no exception, listed or not. The second trap: GFCI protection does not rescue a standard duplex cut face-up into a counter. Protection is not listing.
inspection_fails: Standard duplex cut face-up into an island countertop; the device is not listed for countertop applications — 406.5(G)(1).
Listed pop-up assembly set face-up in the counter area below the sink — 406.5(G)(2) allows no exception there.
Face-up countertop receptacle defended as 'GFCI protected' — protection is not listing, 406.5(G)(1).
Receptacle face-up in a work surface using an assembly listed for wall use only.

In a countertop, but never in the area below a sink

page_quiz.question: Which paragraph bans face-up receptacles below a sink with no listed exception?
page_quiz.explain_plain: (G)(2) is the flat ban: no face-up receptacle in the area below a sink, listed or not.

choices: Violation — the device is not listed for countertop use

sections.title: Receptacles in damp locations
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(A) covers receptacles in damp locations — places that are protected from direct weather but can be damp, such as a covered porch or a carport. Damp is the middle category: not dry indoors, not taking direct rain.
• The receptacle must be weather-resistant (WR) type. On houses and light commercial work that means the 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V devices — the same WR devices 406.9(B) requires in wet locations.
• The enclosure must keep moisture out of the wiring connections when no plug is inserted. A cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out — the flip lid — is the usual way this is met.
• The cover does not have to stay weatherproof while a cord is plugged in. The in-use (bubble) cover belongs to the wet-location rule, 406.9(B).
sections.on_the_job: Covered lanai on a Florida home: the receptacles sit under the roof, but afternoon storms blow mist across them — that is damp, not dry. Fit WR receptacles and flip-lid covers that close weatherproof with nothing plugged in. Look up before you decide: if the device can get rained on with the cover open or closed — past the roof drip line, or under a leaking gutter — treat it as wet, not damp, and use the 406.9(B) arrangement: a WR receptacle plus a listed extra-duty in-use cover. When in doubt, install the wet-location setup — it satisfies the damp case too.
sections.why_it_exists: Damp air, condensation and wind-blown mist corrode contacts and creep across damp surfaces inside a box. A receptacle that is not weather-resistant loses contact pressure and insulation resistance after a few Florida summers, and an enclosure that lets moisture sit on the connections does the same damage from outside. The rule keeps the damp away from the device and its wiring connections.
inspection_fails: Standard (non-WR) receptacle installed on a covered porch or in a carport.
No cover, or a cover that is not weatherproof with the plug removed, so moisture sits in the box.
Receptacle past the roof drip line treated as damp — it takes direct rain and needs the wet-location in-use cover.
Indoor cover plate on a damp-location box, or the gasket missing and the cover hanging open.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is calling a covered porch a dry location. Covered and protected from direct rain is the definition of a damp location, and the receptacle still has to be WR type with a cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out. The other wrong pick is the bubble cover: damp locations do not require an in-use cover — that requirement is 406.9(B), the wet rule.

Be weatherproof when the plug is removed
Be lockable in the closed position
page_quiz.explain_plain: 406.9(A) requires the enclosure to keep moisture out when nothing is plugged in; the flip lid is the usual way.

A GFCI alone makes it compliant
Dry-location parts are fine if GFCI protected
page_quiz.explain_plain: Direct rain makes it a wet location under 406.9(B), which adds the listed extra-duty in-use cover.

sections.title: Receptacles in wet locations — in-use covers and weather-resistant devices
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(B) covers receptacles in wet locations — places where water can reach the device whether or not something is plugged in. Two parts work together:
• The enclosure must stay weatherproof while a plug is inserted and the cord is in use. That is the bubble, or in-use, cover: protection with the plug IN, not just with the cover closed.
• 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V receptacles in wet locations must be weather-resistant (WR) type.
An unattended wet-location receptacle, such as one on a house exterior, needs that in-use protection; the rule has specific treatment for receptacles that are attended while in use.
Two details decide inspections here. First, the in-use cover (the outlet box hood) must be listed and identified as extra duty — the heavier hinged cover — where 406.9(B)(1) requires it; a light flip lid is a damp-location part, not a wet-location one. Second, the WR requirement in this section reaches the 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V receptacles a house and a light commercial job actually use; larger pin-and-sleeve and locking devices follow their own listing for the location.
sections.on_the_job: Stock both parts on the truck: a WR receptacle and an extra-duty in-use cover. A flat flip lid on an exterior receptacle that runs a pump, a charger, or landscape equipment is a correction waiting to happen. Seat the cover gasket fully and route the cord out the bottom notch so the cover can close. On a Florida exterior, assume wet until proven damp: afternoon storms drive rain sideways under most soffits, so the lanai receptacle by the pool equipment gets the WR device and the bubble cover even when the plan just says 'exterior.'
sections.florida_note: Florida note: afternoon rain and irrigation spray make most Florida exterior receptacles wet locations in practice, whatever the plan calls them. Default to WR + in-use cover outside.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: An ordinary receptacle outdoors corrodes: springs and contacts green up, resistance rises, and the device heats or fails — often with a pump or charger plugged in and nobody watching. The WR device is built with corrosion-resistant parts and UV-stable plastics, and the in-use cover keeps driven rain out of the connection while it is actually working, which is when it matters most.
inspection_fails: Flat flip-lid cover on an exterior receptacle in a wet location — weatherproof only with the plug out.
Standard (non-WR) receptacle installed outdoors; no WR marking on the face.
In-use cover not extra duty where 406.9(B)(1) requires it, or gasket not seated so the cover cannot close.
Cord routed out the side of the bubble cover so the lid stands open in the rain.
sections.exam_trap: The trap swaps the two covers. A flip lid is weatherproof only with the plug out — that is the damp-location rule in 406.9(A). A wet location demands weatherproof with the plug inserted, the in-use cover, and the heavy extra-duty version where 406.9(B)(1) applies. Picking 'flip lid' for a wet location is the classic wrong answer — and WR alone does not fix it: the device and the cover are separate requirements.

tables.caption: Damp vs wet at a glance (NEC 2020)
tables.note: Both locations take WR receptacles at 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V.

figures.alt: Elevation of an exterior wet-location receptacle with an extra-duty in-use bubble cover closed over a plugged-in cord, a WR receptacle inside, and the cord leaving through the bottom notch.
figures.caption: Weatherproof with the plug in: WR device plus extra-duty in-use cover.

page_quiz.question: A wet-location receptacle must remain weatherproof:
choices: Only when nothing is plugged in
While a plug is inserted and in use
Only if it is GFCI protected
page_quiz.explain_plain: That is the in-use cover rule: the enclosure stays weatherproof with the plug in and the cord in use. Weatherproof with the plug out is the damp-location standard.

page_quiz.question: Which receptacles in wet locations must be WR type?
choices: 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V
page_quiz.explain_plain: 406.9(B) names the 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V devices — the ones houses and light commercial jobs use. Larger devices follow their own listing.

page_quiz.question: The in-use cover on a wet-location receptacle must be listed and identified as:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Where 406.9(B)(1) requires it, the outlet box hood is the heavier extra-duty cover. A light flip lid is a damp-location part.

sections.title: No receptacles inside the tub or shower zone
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.9(C) keeps receptacles out of the zone directly inside and immediately around a bathtub or shower stall.
• The zone measures 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or the shower stall threshold.
• No receptacle may be installed within that zone. GFCI protection does not change the answer — this is a location rule.
• The receptacle the basin requires still has to be provided; it just has to land outside the zone.
The rule exists because a person in water is in the worst possible position to contact a device or a cord connected to it.
sections.on_the_job: On layout, mark the zone on the floor plan before you place bath receptacles, not at trim. Vanity receptacles belong outside the zone even when the counter runs close to the tub. If the only wall space is inside the zone, move the discussion to the builder before rough-in, not to the inspector at final. On a tight Florida production bath — a tub-and-shower combo beside a long vanity — measure both 3 ft rules before the box is nailed up: the basin receptacle has to be within reach of the basin and still clear of the zone measured from the tub rim.

nec2023_change.change: Clarified receptacle restrictions in and around bathtubs and showers in Section 406.9(C). A new Exception #4 was added to allow single receptacles within 36" of the tub or shower with limitations.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 406.9(C) Bathtub and Shower Space

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 406.9(C): Clarified receptacle restrictions in and around bathtubs and showers in Section 406.9(C). A new Exception #4 was added to allow single receptacles within 36" of the tub or shower with limitations.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Water, bare skin, and a grounded tub or drain make the person in the tub the best conductor in the room. A receptacle inside the zone puts a device and its cord within reach of a wet hand — the hair dryer cord draped toward the water is the classic case. No protective device buys what distance buys, so the Code keeps the receptacle out of reach of the water entirely.
inspection_fails: Receptacle installed inside the tub/shower zone, within 3 ft horizontally of the tub rim.
Zone measured from the faucet or the tub center instead of the top of the rim or threshold.
Vanity receptacle landed in the zone because the counter ran long — never re-measured at rough-in.
Receptacle added inside the zone at trim for a bidet seat or towel warmer without checking 406.9(C).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is “it is GFCI protected, so it can sit by the tub.” Section 406.9(C) is a location rule, not a protection rule: in the 2020 Code no receptacle is permitted inside the zone at all, GFCI or not. Protection never cures a prohibited location — the device has to move, not get a better breaker.

3 ft from the faucet and 8 ft from the drain
8 ft horizontally and 3 ft vertically from the tub center
The entire bathroom is the zone

choices: Nothing — they are the same measurement
The basin rule measures from the basin's outside edge to where the receptacle must reach; the zone measures from the tub rim, space the receptacle must stay out of
The zone is measured in inches, the basin rule in feet

page_quiz.explain_plain: 210.52(D) puts a receptacle within 3 ft of the basin's outside edge; 406.9(C) keeps receptacles 3 ft away from the tub rim or shower threshold. Both have to be satisfied at once.

sections.title: Tamper-resistant receptacles in dwellings and other listed occupancies
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 406.12 requires tamper-resistant receptacles in dwelling units and in a list of other occupancies where children are present, such as guest rooms, childcare and preschool areas, dormitories, and certain medical and office waiting areas. A TR receptacle has internal shutters that only open when both blades of a plug go in together, so a key or paperclip pushed into one slot does not reach a live contact. The requirement applies at the receptacle locations the article covers, generally those at normal reachable height rather than the listed exceptions such as receptacles high above the floor or inside a luminaire.

The exceptions matter on service work. The TR requirement does not reach:
• Receptacles located more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor
• Receptacles that are part of a luminaire or an appliance
• A single receptacle for one appliance, or a duplex for two, in the dedicated space for an appliance that is not easily moved in normal use
• Nongrounding-type replacements installed under 406.4(D) where the box has no grounding means
Everything else at normal device height in the occupancies this section lists is TR — when in doubt, the TR device is the answer.
sections.on_the_job: On a Sharma trim-out in a new Ocala single-family home, every receptacle at normal device height gets a TR device — bedrooms, living areas, kitchen, halls. Protection comes from the dual-function breaker in the Siemens panel (S-07), so the devices are plain TR receptacles, not GFCI receptacles. Two spots on that job are not TR: the single receptacle behind the refrigerator, sitting in its dedicated appliance space, and a receptacle mounted more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor for a wall-mounted TV. On a service call, a TR receptacle with a failed shutter is replaced with another TR device (406.4(D)) — never with a standard receptacle just because it was on the truck.
sections.sharma_note: S-07 pairs with this page: the standard Sharma dwelling device is a TR receptacle, with GFCI/AFCI protection supplied by the DFN breaker rather than by a GFCI receptacle.

nec2023_change.change: The tamper-resistant (TR) list grew to ten location groups, adding boathouses, fitness centers, group homes, rehab facilities, nursing homes, foster care, psychiatric hospitals and farm buildings open to the public. Item (1) now lists boathouses, mobile homes and manufactured homes by name, along with dwelling units and their garages, outbuildings and common areas.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 406.12 Tamper-resistant receptacle locations

sections.why_it_exists: Small children explore with whatever is in their hand — a key, a paperclip, a hairpin. Pushed into one slot of an ordinary receptacle, that metal reaches a live contact and the child becomes the path to ground. The shutters in a TR receptacle stay closed unless both plug blades press in together, so a single object in one slot touches nothing live. The rule puts that protection everywhere children live, sleep, wait, or are cared for.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that TR receptacles are only required in nurseries and children's bedrooms. 406.12 covers dwelling units in all the areas 210.52 specifies, plus the other listed occupancies. The second trap is reading the height exception as 5 ft — the exception starts at more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor.
inspection_fails: Standard (non-TR) receptacle installed in a dwelling bedroom — 406.12 requires tamper-resistant devices.
Damaged TR receptacle replaced with a standard device on a service call.
Non-TR receptacles in a childcare facility playroom.
Receptacle claimed under the height exception but measured at 5 ft above the floor, not more than 5-1/2 ft.
