sections.title: Switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 408 covers the boards themselves: switchboards, switchgear, and the panelboards Sharma installs on nearly every job. For residential and light commercial work, the live parts of this article are:
• The circuit directory: every circuit identified specifically at the board, spares marked as spares (408.4(A)).
• Identification of the source of supply where a board is fed from another board (408.4(B)).
• A short-circuit current rating at least equal to the available fault current (408.6).
• Unused openings closed with closures listed for the enclosure (408.7).
• Overcurrent protection of the panelboard itself, at no more than the panelboard's rating (408.36).
• One grounded (neutral) conductor per terminal (408.41).
• Breakers of the type listed for the panel they sit in.
The industrial switchboard sections matter on larger commercial gear; the directory and listing rules matter everywhere.
sections.on_the_job: Treat the panel as a document, not just a box: directory filled in, circuits identified at every disconnect, unused openings closed, and only listed breakers installed. An inspector can fail a beautiful rough-in on a blank directory. On a Sharma trim, that means a new Siemens board (S-02) with the directory written from the actual schedule and checked circuit by circuit, spares marked 'SPARE,' and every open space closed with the Siemens filler listed for that panel. In an existing Square D panel, only Square D breakers listed for that panel go in (S-03). And check the protection: a 100 A panelboard never sits behind a 200 A breaker just because the feeder is big (408.36).
sections.sharma_note: S-02: all new Sharma gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing Square D panel, install Square D breakers listed for that panel — never mix brands to fill a space.

nec2023_change.change: The enclosure rule now ties to fault current: once available fault current passes 10,000 amps, the panelboard and its enclosure have to be evaluated as a matched combination. If available fault current tops 10,000 amps, the interior and its enclosure need to be evaluated as one combination.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 408.38 Panelboard enclosures and fault current

nec2023_change.change: Two paths for a replacement panelboard in an existing enclosure: listed for that enclosure keeps its rating; if not, it's identified for the use up to 10,000 amps available fault current, field labeled above. Listed for that specific enclosure, by catalog number or dimensions? The replacement keeps its short-circuit current rating (408.9(A)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 408.9 Replacement panelboards in old enclosures

sections.edition_note:
NEC 2023 CHANGE:
• 408.38: The enclosure rule now ties to fault current: once available fault current passes 10,000 amps, the panelboard and its enclosure have to be evaluated as a matched combination. If available fault current tops 10,000 amps, the interior and its enclosure need to be evaluated as one combination.
• 408.9: Two paths for a replacement panelboard in an existing enclosure: listed for that enclosure keeps its rating; if not, it's identified for the use up to 10,000 amps available fault current, field labeled above. Listed for that specific enclosure, by catalog number or dimensions? The replacement keeps its short-circuit current rating (408.9(A)).
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The panelboard is where every circuit in the building starts, and where fault energy is highest. A board protected above its bus rating, fitted with breakers it was never listed for, or left with open spaces becomes the failure point itself. The directory rules exist because the next person — a servicer, a firefighter, a homeowner at midnight — has to kill the right circuit fast, and a wrong label sends them to the wrong breaker.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'Any breaker that snaps into the panel is fine.' It is not. A breaker must be listed for that panelboard — a foreign breaker that physically fits still voids the listing and draws a correction. The companion trap: protecting a 100 A panelboard with a 200 A breaker because the feeder conductors are large. Section 408.36 protects the bus, not the wire.
inspection_fails: Circuit directory blank, generic ('lights,' 'plugs'), or not updated after a circuit change (408.4(A)).
Unused breaker opening left open, or closed with tape instead of a listed filler plate (408.7).
Breaker of another brand installed in the panel — not listed for that panelboard.
100 A panelboard protected by a 200 A overcurrent device (408.36).
Panelboard SCCR below the available fault current at a commercial service (408.6).

sections.title: The circuit directory — specific, on site, and kept current
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.4(A) requires a circuit directory at every panelboard, and identification specific enough to tell the circuits apart:
• Every circuit, and every circuit modification, is legibly identified with a clear, specific description of its purpose or use — the actual load, in the actual building.
• Generic words that fit any house — "plugs," "lights," "bedroom" — do not meet the rule. Neither does a directory copied from the plan or from another job.
• Spare positions are identified as spares.
• The directory is updated whenever circuits are added, moved, or changed.
The directory lives at the board, so the next person who opens the panel can kill the right circuit without guessing.
sections.on_the_job: Fill the directory at trim, from the actual panel schedule, and have the person who wired the house verify it circuit by circuit with a tester or by switching loads on and off. A directory copied from the plan without field verification is how "Kitchen" ends up feeding the water heater. Sharma standard: neat, specific, and correct — "NE bedroom receptacles," not "BR."
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: the directory is part of the finished product the builder sees. Neat, specific, and correct — 'NE bedroom receptacles,' not 'BR.'

nec2023_change.change: Circuit directory rules became a six-part checklist that now requires explaining any abbreviations or symbols. In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 408.4 Circuit directory and source labels

sections.why_it_exists: Troubleshooting and lockout both start at the directory. A wrong or vague label sends a tech to kill "Kitchen" while the water heater stays live, or leaves a crew guessing which breaker feeds the circuit they are about to touch. A specific directory is a safety device that costs nothing but ten honest minutes at trim.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: copying the directory from the plan set, or from the identical house next door. The exam — and the inspector — want the directory that describes this building's circuits as actually wired and verified. "Lights" and "plugs" are the classic wrong answers: they identify nothing, and they distinguish nothing.
inspection_fails: No circuit directory provided at the panelboard (408.4(A)).
Directory entries generic — "plugs," "lights" — the circuits cannot be distinguished from one another.
Spare breaker positions not identified as spares.
Directory not updated after circuits were added or moved.
Directory written for a different building — labels do not match the loads actually fed.

sections.title: Identification of the source of supply
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.4(B) addresses panelboards supplied by a feeder: the board must be marked to identify where its supply comes from when that source is in a different location or is not obvious, so that a person standing at the panel can find the disconnect that kills it.
• The source marking goes at the feeder-supplied panelboard itself.
• The directory rules in 408.4(A) work the other direction: they identify what each circuit in the board feeds.
• Disconnects and circuits are likewise marked for their purpose where it is not self-evident.
The theme of the whole part is that nobody should have to guess what feeds what.
sections.on_the_job: On a sub-panel, label the feeder source (for example, “Fed from Main Panel, Garage”) at the sub-panel and label the feeder breaker at the source panel. Do the same for any panel fed from a generator or a second service, and make the two labels agree with each other. On a Florida house the everyday case is the detached garage or pool-house sub-panel: five minutes at trim decides whether the next tech kills the right breaker on the first try.

sections.why_it_exists: The dangerous panel is the live one nobody can kill. A sub-panel fed from another building, a second service, or a generator can stay energized after the main in front of you is opened — the classic surprise during service work and firefighting. A source marking at the board turns a hunt through the building into one trip to the right disconnect.
inspection_fails: Feeder-fed panelboard with no identification of its source of supply.
Sub-panel in a detached building, with nothing naming the panel or building that feeds it.
Source labels at the two ends disagree — the sub-panel names a source the main panel does not.
Panel fed from a generator or second service, not marked to show the other source.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is marking the circuit directory and calling the panel identified. The directory in 408.4(A) says what each circuit feeds; 408.4(B) answers the other direction — what feeds this panel, and where that source sits. A perfect directory on a feeder-fed board with no source marking still leaves the next person guessing which building, main, or generator keeps it live.

sections.title: The equipment's short-circuit current rating must cover the available fault current
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.6 requires switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards to have a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) at least equal to the available fault current where they are installed. A panel that matches the job on volts and amps can still be the wrong panel if its SCCR is below the fault current the service can deliver into a short.
• The SCCR is marked on the equipment. The available fault current comes from the utility or the design documents — it is not a number you estimate in the field.
• At service equipment in other than dwelling units, the available fault current and the date of the calculation must be field-marked on the equipment (110.24).
• The breakers inside the gear carry interrupting ratings of their own (110.9). The gear's SCCR and the devices' interrupting ratings both have to cover the same fault current.
This requirement was added in the 2020 edition, which is why older change-out habits never asked the question.
sections.on_the_job: Small commercial service change in Orlando: the utility letter puts the available fault current at 22,000 A at the new 400 A service. The value panel on the truck is marked 10 kA SCCR — it cannot go in, even though its bus rating and voltage match. Per S-02 the replacement gear is Siemens, selected with an SCCR of 22 kA or higher, and both numbers — 22,000 A available and the gear's marked SCCR — go in the job file before the gear is ordered. If the fault current is unknown, that is an engineering question for Mike, not a field estimate.
sections.sharma_note: S-02 pairs with this page: new Sharma gear is Siemens, and the SCCR check is part of selecting it, not an afterthought at inspection.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A bolted fault lets the service deliver thousands of amps in a fraction of a cycle. Gear whose SCCR is below that current can rupture, vent molten metal, or blow its doors instead of riding through the fault until the overcurrent device clears it. The rating is what stands between a cleared fault and an exploding enclosure.
inspection_fails: Panelboard installed where the available fault current exceeds its marked SCCR (408.6).
Gear ordered and set before the available fault current was obtained from the utility.
No fault current documented in the job file — nothing to compare the SCCR against.
Available fault current not marked at the service equipment, or the marking left out of date after a utility change (110.24).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer reads the panel's ampere rating as its fault rating: 'a 200 A panel on a 200 A service handles the fault.' Bus amps and SCCR are different numbers. A 200 A panel marked 10 kA SCCR still fails on a service that can deliver 22,000 A of fault current.

sections.title: Unused openings must be closed
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.7 requires unused openings in a panelboard, switchboard or switchgear to be closed with closures that give protection substantially equal to the wall of the enclosure.
• A spare breaker space with no breaker in it is an unused opening: it takes the manufacturer's listed filler plate or blank.
• An unused knockout in the enclosure wall is the same problem in a smaller hole: close it with a listed knockout closure.
• Tape is not a closure. Neither are cardboard, foam, or a near-fit plate from another brand.
An open space is an exposed live-part opening, a dust and vermin path, and an automatic correction on inspection.
sections.on_the_job: Keep listed filler plates for the panel brand on the trim truck. Before final, open every panel, run a finger check for open spaces, blank plates, and missing knock-out closures, and close them with the manufacturer's part. On a Sharma job the panel is Siemens, so the fillers on the truck are Siemens fillers: a near-fit plate from another brand is a correction waiting to happen (S-02/S-03).
sections.sharma_note: S-02/S-03 apply to the closure as well: use the filler listed for that panel, not a near-fit from another brand.
sections.why_it_exists: The bus behind the deadfront stays live even where no breaker is installed. An open space lets fingers, a dropped screwdriver or a curious kid reach it, and it lets dust and roaches build up on the bus until tracking and a short do the rest. A closure as strong as the enclosure wall keeps the box a box.
inspection_fails: Spare breaker space left open with no filler plate: live bus exposed behind the deadfront.
Duct tape or cardboard over an unused opening. Neither is a closure.
Unused knockout in the side of the panel never closed.
Filler plate from a different panel brand forced into the space: not the listed closure for that panel.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating an empty breaker space as harmless because nothing is connected to it. The opening itself is the violation: the live bus stab sits right behind it. 'We will add a breaker later' does not close the hole today.

sections.title: The panelboard itself must be protected
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.36 requires a panelboard to be protected by an overcurrent device rated no higher than the panelboard's rating, located within the panelboard or at any point ahead of it on the supply side. In plain terms, a 100 A panel may not sit behind a 200 A breaker just because the feeder wires are large. The bus has its own limit and something must enforce it. The exceptions are narrow:
• Exception No. 1: service equipment with multiple disconnecting means under 230.71 (the split-bus case); with three or more mains, they may not supply a second bus structure.
• Exception No. 2: two main breakers or two sets of fuses on the supply side with a combined rating not over the panelboard rating — and no more than 42 overcurrent devices in the board, counting a 2-pole as two and a 3-pole as three.
• Exception No. 3: existing panelboards used as service equipment for an individual residential occupancy.
A panelboard supplied from a transformer under 240.21(C) gets its protection on the secondary side — in a separate enclosure ahead of the board, or in the board itself (408.36(B)).
sections.on_the_job: When you set a sub-panel, check three numbers together: panel bus rating, feeder conductor ampacity, and the breaker feeding it. The smallest applicable limit governs. Record all three on the panel schedule for the office file. Sharma's light-commercial habit: a 100 A Siemens sub-panel gets a 100 A feeder breaker even when the feeder conductors could carry more — the breaker is protecting the bus, not just the wire.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Feeder conductors are sized for the load and the run; a panelboard bus is built for its rating and nothing more. Put a 100 A bus behind a 200 A breaker and an overload inside the board can push twice the bus rating through stabs and bus bars that were never built for it — the breaker sits happy while the panel cooks. Section 408.36 makes the board's own rating a ceiling that some device, in the board or ahead of it, must enforce.
inspection_fails: 100 A main-lug panelboard fed from a 200 A breaker — board protected above its rating (408.36).
Replacement main breaker rated higher than the panelboard bus it protects.
Two-main exception claimed on a board holding more than 42 overcurrent devices.
Transformer-fed panelboard whose only protection is on the primary side (408.36(B)).

sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'the feeder is 200 A wire, so a 200 A breaker ahead of a 100 A panel is fine — the wire is protected.' The wire is; the panelboard is not. Section 408.36 protects the panelboard at its own rating. The reverse trap is calling every split-bus service a violation — the 230.71 multiple-disconnect arrangement is Exception No. 1, not a defect.

sections.title: Each grounded (neutral) conductor gets its own terminal
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.41 requires each grounded conductor in a panelboard to terminate in its own individual terminal that is not used for any other conductor, unless the terminal is specifically identified for more than one.
• One grounded (neutral) conductor per terminal. Doubling two neutrals under one screw is a classic correction.
• The hazard is mechanical: when one circuit is worked on, loosening the shared terminal can open the neutral of a live circuit sharing it.
• Equipment grounding conductors follow their own termination rules and the panel's listing; the one-per-terminal discipline on this page is about the grounded conductors.
sections.on_the_job: At trim, land neutrals one to a screw and torque them; never park a second neutral under a screw 'temporarily.' On a panel change-out — new gear is Siemens per S-02 — budget the time to separate doubled neutrals: an older Florida panel typically hides several, and finding them is part of the job. The directory update in 408.4(A) happens on the same visit.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A shared neutral terminal is a single point of failure for two circuits. Back one screw out to move a circuit and the other circuit loses its neutral while it is still hot — on a multiwire branch circuit the loads end up in series across 240 V and electronics burn. Even without that, two conductors under one screw seat unevenly, loosen over time, and heat.
inspection_fails: Two grounded (neutral) conductors under one terminal screw in the panelboard (408.41).
Grounded conductor landed with another conductor in a terminal not identified for more than one conductor (408.41).
Doubled neutrals left in place through a panel change-out.
Neutral terminal screws backed off or untorqued after circuits were moved during service work.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating neutrals like grounds: 'two under one screw is fine — the bar is all one piece anyway.' Section 408.41 is written about grounded conductors, one per terminal, and a terminal specifically identified for more than one conductor is the only way out. Doubling neutrals because they land on the same bar is the write-up.

page_quiz.question: Two neutrals are landed under one screw on the neutral bar. Verdict?
choices: OK if both circuits are on the same breaker

page_quiz.explain_plain: 408.41 requires each grounded conductor to terminate in an individual terminal not used for any other conductor.

sections.title: A panelboard may not be installed face-up
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 408.43 prohibits installing a panelboard in a face-up position. A load center belongs on a vertical surface with its breakers oriented as the listing intends; a face-up board collects debris and water, and its breakers do not operate or indicate as designed. The rule was added in the 2020 edition and most often matters on custom commercial millwork and unusual equipment layouts, not on a standard house panel.
• Legal: the panelboard's front faces a wall — breakers in their listed, vertical orientation.
• Banned since 2020: face-up, front pointing at the ceiling.
• Still legal under the 2020 book, banned in 2023: face-down, front pointing at the floor — see the edition note.
sections.on_the_job: If a plan or a cabinet detail shows a panel lying flat, stop at rough-in and raise it with the builder — the fix is a layout change, not a field workaround. Check orientation on any pre-built equipment package before it is set. On a Sharma commercial job, the millwork detail for a coffee-bar cabinet showed the load center flat under the counter: the cabinet grew a vertical section at rough-in, the panel went on it upright, and the directory (408.4(A)) stayed readable standing in front of it.

nec2023_change.change: Panelboards can't be installed facing down now. Added to the 2020 face-up ban, a panelboard's front can point neither at the ceiling nor at the floor. A panelboard can't be mounted face-down, with its front pointing at the floor, such as on the underside of a ceiling or platform.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 408.43 Panelboards can't face up or down

sections.why_it_exists: A panelboard is a listed assembly tested in one orientation. Lay it face-up and the gutter becomes a tray: dust, screws, water and whatever the next trade drops all land on live parts and breaker mechanisms. Breakers lying flat also do not trip, reset or read the way their listing assumes. The rule keeps the equipment in the only position it was ever evaluated in.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'face-up is fine if the cover stays on' — 408.43 bans the position outright, cover or not. The subtler trap is the calendar: face-down is banned only in the 2023 edition. On a 2020 permit a face-down board is bad practice but not a 408.43 violation; on a 2023 permit it fails.

Flat-mounted board with debris and water standing in the gutter at rough-in inspection.

page_quiz.question: A panelboard mounted face-down under a platform is —
choices: Legal if it has a cover
page_quiz.explain_plain: 2020 banned face-up only. The 2023 edition added the face-down ban to 408.43 — check which book the permit is under.

page_quiz.question: Why does 408.43 care about orientation?
choices: A face-up board collects debris and water, and breakers do not operate or indicate as listed
The directory is harder to print
Panels are only sold for walls
page_quiz.explain_plain: The listing assumes a vertical board. Flat, the gutter traps debris and water and the breakers leave their evaluated position.

sections.title: Industrial control panels — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 409 covers industrial control panels: the factory- or field-assembled panels that control industrial machinery and equipment. The article sets the rules for the panel's short-circuit current rating (SCCR) marking, supply conductor sizing, and internal wiring and grounding.
• The SCCR is the headline item. The panel must be marked with it (409.110), and a panel may not be installed where the available fault current at its supply exceeds the rating marked on it.
• Read the label before the panel is set: supply voltage, phases, full-load current, and SCCR all come off the manufacturer's marking.
• Supply conductors are sized from the panel's marked ratings, and the panel's grounding follows 409.60.
Sharma meets this article on light commercial and equipment work rather than in houses — rooftop equipment, lift stations, and machine controls.
sections.on_the_job: Read the SCCR on the panel label and compare it with the available fault current at its supply before you set the panel. On a light-commercial equipment swap in Orlando, the utility letter put the available fault current at 22 kA. The replacement control panel's label read 10 kA SCCR — that panel does not get set, no matter that its breakers are rated 22 kA; the assembly's marked SCCR is the ceiling. A panel marked 65 kA SCCR clears the same supply with room to spare. If the panel has no SCCR marking or the fault current is unknown, stop and take it to Mike — that is an engineering check, not a field guess.

nec2023_change.change: Section 409.60 for industrial control panels was restructured, creating (A) Grounding and (B) Bonding.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 409.60 Bonding

nec2023_change.change: New Section 409.70 has been added requiring surge protection for industrial control panels.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 409.70 Surge Protection

sections.why_it_exists: A short circuit does not ask permission. If the fault current at a panel is higher than the panel was built and tested to withstand, the failure is not a tripped breaker — it is bus bars tearing loose, contacts welding, and an enclosure coming apart in front of whoever is standing there. The SCCR marking is the panel's tested ceiling, and the available fault current is the number it has to beat.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is the breaker's interrupting rating: 'The main breaker is rated 22 kA, so the panel is good for 22 kA.' The breaker's AIC is one component's rating. The panel's SCCR is the tested rating of the whole assembly — the weakest part sets it — and 409.110 makes the marked SCCR the number the installation is judged against.
inspection_fails: Industrial control panel installed where the available fault current exceeds the SCCR marked on the panel (409.110).
Panel set with a missing or illegible SCCR marking — the ceiling was never checked.
Field modifications inside a listed panel that void its listing and its SCCR.
On a job permitted under the NEC 2023, an industrial control panel with no surge protection (409.70).

sections.title: Industrial control panels — marking and short-circuit current rating (409.110)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 409.110 requires every industrial control panel to be marked with its electrical ratings, the way a motor carries a nameplate:
• The manufacturer's name or trademark.
• Input voltage and number of phases.
• Full-load current.
• The short-circuit current rating — the SCCR.
The SCCR is a ceiling, not a suggestion: the panel may not be installed where the available fault current at its supply exceeds the marked rating. A panel that matches the job on voltage and amps can still be the wrong panel. Read the label before the panel is set. A missing or illegible SCCR is a stop-and-ask, not a guess. Switchboards and panelboards carry the same idea under 408.6.
sections.on_the_job: Light-commercial equipment swap in Orlando: the utility letter puts the available fault current at the service at 22 kA. The replacement control panel's label reads the right voltage and phases — and SCCR 10 kA. That panel does not get set, even though the breakers inside it are rated 22 kA: the assembly's marked SCCR governs, not the highest-rated part inside. Photograph the label with the rest of the nameplates, and if the SCCR comes up short, that is an engineering conversation with the office before the panel is set, not after.
sections.figure_idea: Sample panel label with the SCCR line circled next to voltage and phase.
sections.why_it_exists: When a fault hits, a panel has to survive the energy the service can deliver until a breaker clears it. A panel whose SCCR sits below the available fault current can come apart instead of just tripping. The marking rule puts the one number that decides "can this panel live here" on the panel itself, where the installer reads it before the panel is bolted down — not after the fault.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: "The breakers inside are rated 22 kA, so the panel is good for 22 kA of fault current." No. The panel's rating is the SCCR marked on its label under 409.110. Strong parts inside do not raise the assembly rating — the marked SCCR is the ceiling for the whole panel.
inspection_fails: Control panel installed where the available fault current exceeds its marked SCCR (409.110).
Panel set with the SCCR marking missing or illegible — the rating was never verified.
Panel supplied at a voltage or phase arrangement different from its 409.110 marking.
Available fault current for the location never obtained or recorded before the panel was set.

figures.alt: A sample industrial control panel label with the four 409.110 markings and the SCCR line highlighted, compared against 22 kA of available fault current: a 10 kA panel may not be set, a 65 kA panel may.
figures.caption: Read the label: the SCCR line decides if the panel can live here.

page_quiz.question: Available fault current at a panel's supply is 22 kA. The panel label reads SCCR 10 kA. May the panel be installed?
choices: Yes — its breakers are rated 22 kA
Yes — SCCR is only a marking
No — the marked SCCR is below the available fault current
Only if a fuse is added ahead of it
page_quiz.explain_plain: The marked SCCR is a ceiling. Where the available fault current exceeds it, the panel may not be installed.

page_quiz.question: Which item is NOT part of the 409.110 marking?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 409.110 marks the panel with its electrical ratings: manufacturer, input voltage and phases, full-load current, and SCCR.

page_quiz.question: The SCCR line on a panel label is missing or illegible. The correct action is to:
choices: Guess the rating from the breakers inside
Stop and get the rating before the panel is set
page_quiz.explain_plain: A missing SCCR is a stop-and-ask. The rating comes from the manufacturer's marking, not from the parts inside.

sections.title: Luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 410 covers light fixtures in the broad code sense: luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — where they may be installed, how they are supported, temperature limits near combustible material, and the special zones in bathtubs, showers, and clothes closets. The parts Sharma hits constantly:
• The tub and shower zone (410.10(D)): 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold. Inside it, a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where shower spray hits it. Pendants, hanging fixtures, and ceiling-suspended fans are not permitted in the zone at all.
• Clothes closets (410.16): clearances are measured from the closet storage space — 12 in for a surface-mounted enclosed incandescent or LED fixture, 6 in for surface fluorescent and for recessed fixtures. Open-lamp incandescent fixtures and pendants are not permitted at any clearance.
• Recessed fixtures: insulation contact and thermal protection (410.116).
Fixture listing and its instructions (110.3(B)) do half the work in this article — the box and the spec sheet are part of the code answer.
sections.on_the_job: Read the fixture's own listing before you rough the box: weight, temperature rating, damp/wet rating, and closet or shower suitability are all on the label or the cut sheet, not in the field manual. On a Florida master bath, mark the 3 ft by 8 ft zone on the plan at rough-in: the architect's shower light inside it must be the listed wet-location model, and the vanity fixtures sit outside the zone. In the closet, default to an enclosed LED fixture, surface-mounted at 12 in clear of the storage space — never a pendant or an exposed lamp.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma bath practice (company practice, not 410): vanity lighting plus the architect's wet-location shower light, with no extra general ceiling light added by habit. Follow the plan; do not add or delete bath lights on your own.

nec2023_change.change: Cord-connected grow lights on circuits over 150 volts to ground, like 277 volts, now need a listed special-purpose GFCI (SPGFCI). The rule also now spells out which cords trigger it. Grow lights on a circuit over 150 volts to ground, such as 277 volts from a 480Y/277 system, must be protected by a listed SPGFCI.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 410.184 Grow light GFCI and SPGFCI

The rule moved from 410.130(G) to 410.71. Indoors outside dwellings, a disconnect is now required on LED luminaires that use double-ended lamps and have field-serviceable drivers (410.71(1)).
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 410.71 LED and fluorescent fixture disconnects

sections.why_it_exists: Fixtures make heat inches from the things that burn — clothes on a closet rod, insulation over a recessed can — and they hang over water where people stand wet and barefoot. The zone and clearance rules keep hot lamps off combustibles and keep the wrong fixture types out of reach of a person in a tub.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'A pendant is fine in the closet if it hangs 12 in from the storage space.' Clearance never rescues a banned type — 410.16(B) bars pendant luminaires and open or partially enclosed incandescent lamps in clothes closets outright. The second trap is measuring closet clearances from the wall or the clothes instead of from the storage space the Code defines.
inspection_fails: Pendant or open-lamp fixture installed in a clothes closet (410.16(B)).
Closet fixture closer than 12 in (surface) or 6 in (recessed) to the storage space (410.16(C)).
Damp-only fixture installed where shower spray hits it inside the tub/shower zone (410.10(D)).
Ceiling-suspended fan installed inside the tub/shower zone (410.10(D)).
Fixture installed against its listing instructions — wrong location rating (110.3(B)).

sections.title: Luminaires in the bathtub and shower zone
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 410.10(D) controls luminaires inside the bathtub and shower zone — the space measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold.
• Inside the zone, a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where it is subject to shower spray.
• Some types are not permitted in the zone at all, including hanging luminaires, pendants, and ceiling-suspended fans.
• A luminaire outside the zone is not governed by this subsection, even if it is in the same bathroom.
sections.on_the_job: Mark the zone on the plan at rough-in and check every bath fixture against it, including the shower light and any fan/light combo. Confirm the damp or wet marking on the fixture label matches where it actually sits, and keep the label information in the job file. Watch the fan/light combo centered over a tub-shower: the fan makes the fixture a ceiling-suspended fan — a type the zone prohibits — even when its light half is wet-listed. The whole fixture has to be a type the zone allows, in the listing the location requires.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note: the architect's specified shower light is the fixture of record — install the listed wet-location model specified, not a damp-only substitute from stock.

sections.why_it_exists: A fixture over a tub or inside a shower lives in steam and direct spray, within reach of a wet person standing in water. The listing rules keep water away from the fixture's live parts, and the banned types are the ones that hang down into reach — a pendant a bather can grab, or a fan hanging over the water.
inspection_fails: Pendant or hanging luminaire installed over the tub, inside the zone.
Damp-location luminaire installed where shower spray reaches it — a wet-location listing is required.
Ceiling-suspended fan, or fan/light combo, installed over a tub-shower inside the zone.
Fixture listing label not available at inspection, so the damp or wet rating could not be verified.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is answering from the room instead of from the zone: “the whole bathroom needs wet-listed fixtures,” or the reverse, “the pendant is wet-listed, so it may hang over the tub.” Location decides first. Outside the zone, this subsection does not apply at all; inside it, a prohibited type stays prohibited no matter what its listing says.

sections.title: Luminaires in clothes closets — permitted types and clearances
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 410.16 controls what may light a clothes closet and how far it must sit from the closet storage space — the volume defined in 410.2:
• Storage space: 24 inches out from the side and back walls, from the floor up to 6 feet or the highest clothes-hanging rod; then 12 inches out from the walls, or the width of the shelf if greater, from there up to the ceiling.
• Permitted [410.16(A)]: surface-mounted or recessed incandescent or LED luminaires with a completely enclosed light source; surface-mounted or recessed fluorescent luminaires; and surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaires identified as suitable for installation within the closet storage space.
• Not permitted [410.16(B)]: incandescent luminaires with open or partially enclosed lamps, and pendant luminaires or lampholders.
• Minimum clearances from the nearest point of the storage space [410.16(C)]: 12 inches for a surface-mounted incandescent or LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source, on the ceiling or the wall above the door; 6 inches for a surface-mounted fluorescent in the same positions; 6 inches for a recessed incandescent or LED with a completely enclosed light source; and 6 inches for a recessed fluorescent.
• A surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaire identified for use within the closet storage space may be installed inside the storage space itself [410.16(C)(5)].
sections.on_the_job: Measure the clearance from the storage space, not from the wall or the clothes — that 24-inch and 12-inch volume exists on paper even in an empty closet. The Sharma default is an enclosed LED fixture: surface-mounted on the ceiling at 12 inches clear of the storage space, or recessed at 6 inches, and never a pendant or an exposed lamp in a closet. Check the shelf before placing the fixture: a shelf wider than 12 inches pushes the top of the storage space out with it.
sections.why_it_exists: A closet is a box full of fuel: clothes, blankets, and boxes stacked toward the ceiling. A hot or bare lamp touching fabric, or a broken lamp dropping hot parts onto clothes, starts a fire behind a closed door where nobody sees it. The clearances keep the heat off the stored material, and the enclosed-source rule keeps lamp parts off it too.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer measures the 12 inches from the wall. Clearances run from the nearest point of the closet storage space — the paper volume in 410.2 — whether or not clothes are hanging there yet. Second trap pick: a pendant is fine if its lamp is enclosed. It is not; pendants are prohibited outright.
inspection_fails: Pendant luminaire or bare lampholder in a clothes closet (410.16(B)).
Surface-mounted LED fixture 8 in. from the storage space where 12 in. is the minimum (410.16(C)).
Open-lamp incandescent fixture mounted over the closet shelf.
Clearance measured from the wall instead of from the 410.2 storage space.

sections.title: Recessed luminaires — insulation contact and thermal protection
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 410.116 covers recessed luminaires — the cans and downlights that sit inside ceilings:
• Combustible clearance — 410.116(A)(1): a fixture not identified for insulation contact keeps its recessed parts at least 1/2 in from combustible material. Points of support and the trim at the ceiling opening may touch.
• Insulation clearance — 410.116(A)(2): unless the fixture is Type IC, thermal insulation may not be installed above the fixture or within 3 in of its enclosure, wiring compartment, ballast, transformer, LED driver, or power supply.
• Type IC fixtures are identified for direct contact with insulation, and may touch insulation and combustible material.
• Thermal protection: recessed fixtures are thermally protected — a sensor shuts the fixture down if it overheats — except where the fixture is identified as inherently protected.
The IC rating belongs to the specific fixture and is printed on its label. It is never a property of recessed fixtures in general.
sections.on_the_job: Florida attic, blown insulation going in over a finished ceiling: read every housing label at rough-in, before the ceiling closes. Type IC cans can be buried. A non-IC can needs its 3 in of clear air and 1/2 in from combustibles — in blown insulation that means a dam or cover that survives the insulation crew. Flag it at rough-in, while the fix is still cheap, not after the blower truck leaves.
sections.why_it_exists: A recessed can is a heat source sealed inside a wood-framed ceiling. Insulation that belongs everywhere else in a Florida attic traps that heat against framing and wiring. The clearances keep an air path around a non-IC fixture, and thermal protection is the backstop that kills the light before the heat does damage. An IC rating moves the protection into the fixture itself, so the ceiling can be insulated tight without cooking the can.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: "All modern LED cans are IC rated, so insulation can touch any of them." The IC rating belongs to the specific fixture and is printed on its label — plenty of cans are non-IC. The reverse trap cuts the other way: a non-IC fixture is not banned from an insulated ceiling. It just has to keep its clearances.
inspection_fails: Non-IC recessed fixture buried in blown insulation — no 3 in clearance (410.116(A)(2)).
Recessed parts of a non-IC fixture against combustible framing — less than 1/2 in clearance (410.116(A)(1)).
Fixture with no Type IC marking installed in direct contact with insulation.
Thermal protection defeated or bypassed after repeated shutoffs.

sections.title: Lighting systems operating at 30 volts or less — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 411 covers lighting systems operating at 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC or less — and only 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC where contact with water is likely. It covers the listed system as a package: the power supply, the fixtures, and the secondary wiring between them.
• Listed system: the system is installed as a listed assembly — a complete listed system, or one assembled from listed parts (411.4). Loose parts gathered in the field do not make an Article 411 system.
• Power supply: the listed power source limits the secondary circuit — the article caps secondary output at 25 amperes.
• Secondary wiring: the conductors on the load side of the power supply follow Article 411's own rules, not ordinary branch-circuit wiring rules.
• Locations: bare-conductor systems are not concealed and do not run through walls, floors or ceilings unless the specific listed system permits it, and the secondary wiring stays out of the pool zone — not within 10 ft of pools, spas, fountains or similar locations unless Article 680 permits it (411.5).
Sharma meets this article mainly in landscape-style and specialty accent lighting inside a project.
sections.on_the_job: A Lake Nona lanai job: the owner wants 24 V DC LED accent lighting around a covered patio that sits near the pool. Spec the listed system — the manufacturer's listed driver, cable and fixtures as one family. The driver is rated 100 W at 24 V DC; the tape and puck runs total 72 W, inside the rating. Route the secondary so the nearest fixture stays 12 ft from the pool water — outside the 10 ft limit in 411.5 — and keep the driver accessible in the garage, not buried in the soffit.
sections.why_it_exists: Thirty volts sounds harmless, so these systems get treated like doorbell wire. But a secondary that can deliver up to 25 amperes will heat a bad splice or an undersized conductor until something chars. The listing is the protection: the power supply, cable and fixtures were tested together, with the supply limiting what a fault can draw. Field-assembled parts have no tested limit.
inspection_fails: Unlisted power supply and tape installed as a 'system' — no listing for the assembly (411.4).
Secondary conductors concealed in the wall with no listed system permitting it (411.5).
Low-voltage fixtures within 10 ft of pool water with no Article 680 basis (411.5).
Secondary splices buried in mulch or underground where the listing does not allow them.
Power supply inaccessible — sealed above a closed soffit.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is '30 volts or less means wire it like a doorbell — any parts, any method.' An Article 411 system is a listed system: a random driver and a roll of tape bought online is not one, no matter how low the voltage. The second trap is the pool: within 10 ft of the water the location rules bite, and where contact with water is likely the ceiling drops to 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC.

sections.title: Low-voltage lighting systems — where they may and may not go (Article 411)
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 411 covers lighting systems operating at not more than 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC (411.1) — the listed low-voltage systems behind a lot of LED tape, under-cabinet, and accent work. Section 411.4 itself is the listing rule:
• The system must be listed as a complete system, or assembled from listed parts. A loose power supply and a roll of tape bought online is not an Article 411 system.
• The power source limits the secondary circuit: the article caps secondary output at 25 amperes.
• Where contact with water is likely, the limits drop to 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC (411.1).
The location limits live in 411.5:
• Bare-conductor systems are not concealed and do not run through walls, floors, or ceilings unless the specific listed system permits it.
• Secondary wiring is not concealed or extended through a building wall, floor, or ceiling unless it is wired with a Chapter 3 method, or with Class 2 wiring where the power supply is Class 2.
• The system stays at least 10 ft from pools, spas, fountains, and similar locations unless Article 680 permits it.
sections.on_the_job: Spec the listed system — power supply, cable, and fixtures from one listed family — and keep the driver accessible. Inspectors ask whose system it is; 'the homeowner bought it online' is not an answer. On the Lake Nona lanai job the pattern held: a listed 24 V DC driver rated 100 W feeding tape and puck runs totaling 72 W, inside the rating with room to spare, and the secondary routed so the nearest fixture stays 12 ft from the pool water — outside the 10 ft limit in 411.5. The driver went in an accessible spot, not buried behind the tile.

sections.why_it_exists: Low voltage feels harmless, so it gets installed casually — unlisted drivers buried in walls, bare tape stapled where hands and water reach. The listing rule makes one manufacturer answer for the whole chain: supply, cable, and fixtures tested together. The location limits keep a system nobody thinks of as 'wiring' from being hidden like wiring, or from reaching the pool zone.

Driver buried inside a closed wall or above a sealed ceiling where it cannot be reached for service.

Low-voltage accent fixtures 6 ft from the pool water with no Article 680 basis, 411.5.
Secondary cable extended through an exterior wall in plain cord instead of a Chapter 3 or Class 2 method, 411.5.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating 30 volts as 'not real wiring,' so any parts on hand will do. The exam answer is the listing: a complete listed system, or listed parts assembled as a system. A loose online power supply plus unlisted tape fails 411.4 before any location question is even reached — and the 25 A secondary cap and the 10 ft pool clearance still apply to the listed system.

sections.title: Appliances — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 422 covers appliances: water heaters, dishwashers, disposals, ranges and cooktops, dryers as appliances, space heaters that plug or hard-wire as appliances, and similar equipment. Its working parts:
• Branch-circuit sizing from the appliance's marked rating; an individual branch circuit — one appliance only — is the default for the big fixed appliances (422.10).
• Overcurrent protection: where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs. An unmarked single non-motor appliance rated over 13.3 A may be protected at up to 150 percent of its rating (422.11(E)).
• Storage water heaters of 120 gallons or less: the branch circuit is sized at 125 percent of the nameplate — a continuous load (422.13).
• GFCI protection that travels with the appliance, wherever it is installed: dishwashers, sump pumps, vending machines, and the rest of the 422.5(A) list.
• A disconnecting means that lets a servicer kill the appliance safely (422.31).
Where an appliance is also a motor load or also HVAC equipment, Articles 430 and 440 may govern instead or in addition — check the appliance's own article first.
sections.on_the_job: For every appliance on a job, settle three things from the nameplate before rough-in is closed: circuit size, cord-and-plug or hard-wired, and where the disconnect will be. The nameplate, not the catalog photo, is the source. Worked example, the standard Florida water heater: 4,500 W at 240 V draws 18.75 A; at 125 percent that is 23.4 A, so it lands on a 30 A circuit with 10 AWG copper. The dishwasher gets its GFCI protection because 422.5 names the appliance — on Sharma work the dual-function breaker supplies it. The microwave gets its own 20 A circuit (S-06).
sections.sharma_note: S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit and is not lumped onto a circuit shared with the hood or anything else. The wire (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA) is not settled until Mike Holt rules.

sections.why_it_exists: Appliances are the loads that run unattended — a water heater recovering a tank at 3 a.m., a dishwasher cycling while the house is empty. Sized wrong, the circuit cooks slowly inside a wall; serviced without a disconnect, the appliance stays live in the tech's hands. The article ties circuit, protection, and disconnect to the one document that knows the load: the nameplate.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: size the water heater circuit at 100 percent of nameplate 'because it is just a resistance load.' Section 422.13 treats a fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less as a continuous load — 125 percent. The 4,500 W heater's 18.75 A becomes a 23.4 A minimum, so the 20 A answer fails before the breaker is even picked.

Breaker larger than the appliance's marked maximum overcurrent device (422.11).

Microwave sharing a circuit with the range hood or another load (Sharma S-06).

sections.title: GFCI protection required for specific appliances
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.5 names the appliances that must have Class A GFCI protection for personnel wherever they are installed. The duty travels with the appliance. It sits on top of the room rules in 210.8, and meeting one does not erase the other.
• Scope: appliances rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single- or 3-phase, cord-and-plug-connected or hardwired. 210.8(D) points to this same list.
• The 2020 list at 422.5(A): automotive vacuum machines; drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations; cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washing machines; tire inflation machines; vending machines; sump pumps; and dishwashers.
• NEC 2020 removed the 'provided for public use' condition and added sump pumps.
• The protection must be readily accessible. 422.5(B) allows five places for it: the branch-circuit overcurrent device; a device or outlet within the supply circuit; an integral part of the attachment plug; within the supply cord not more than 12 in. from the attachment plug; or factory-installed within the appliance.
• Edition caution: wider appliance lists circulating from NEC 2023 research are not the 2020 list. In 2020, ranges, dryers, and microwaves pick up their GFCI duties through the location rules in 210.8, not through 422.5.
sections.on_the_job: Check an appliance against both lists: 210.8 for the room and receptacle, and 422.5 for the appliance itself. The everyday Sharma case is the dishwasher in a new Marion County kitchen — 422.5(A) names dishwashers, so it needs GFCI wherever the kitchen sits. On Sharma work the dual-function breaker usually supplies this protection for a 120 V appliance circuit (S-07); confirm the breaker type actually provides GFCI, not AFCI only. A sump pump in a garage pit is the second everyday case: hardwired or cord-and-plug, it is on the list either way.
sections.sharma_note: S-07: every 120V breaker on new Sharma work is dual-function AFCI/GFCI, which is what makes the breaker the protection point for these appliances.
sections.figure_idea: Seven appliance icons in a row — vacuum, water cooler, spray washer, tire inflator, vending machine, sump pump, dishwasher — each wearing a GFCI badge.

nec2023_change.source: Georgia DCA 2023 NEC changes presentation

sections.why_it_exists: These appliances are used with wet hands, on wet floors, or around water: a dishwasher in a kitchen, a sump pump standing in a flooded pit, a spray washer on a wash pad. A ground fault can put the metal case at line voltage and send current through the person touching it. Class A GFCI senses that small leak and opens the circuit before the current through the person can kill.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer builds the list from 2023: it adds electric ranges, clothes dryers, and microwave ovens to 422.5. Under the 2020 Code those appliances pick up GFCI duties only through the location rules in 210.8 — the 422.5(A) list has seven appliances. The pick candidates forget is the sump pump, added in 2020.

Sump pump plugged into an unprotected receptacle — 'it is only a pump' is not an exception.

Vending machine cord-and-plug connected with no GFCI in the plug, the cord, or the circuit.

sections.title: Branch circuits for appliances (422.10)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.10 starts appliance work with the circuit: the branch circuit must be sized for the appliance it serves, using the appliance's marked rating, and an individual branch circuit — one that supplies only that appliance — is the default pattern for the big fixed appliances. Where two or more appliances share a circuit, this section's load rules and the general rules of Articles 210 and 220 both apply. The numbers that ride with it:
• Where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs (422.11)
• A single non-motor appliance rated over 13.3 A, not marked with a maximum, may be protected at up to 150 percent of its rating; at 13.3 A or less the ceiling is 20 A (422.11(E))
• A fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less is sized at 125 percent of nameplate — a continuous load (422.13)
When the nameplate and the circuit disagree, the circuit gets corrected; the appliance does not get derated by hope.
sections.on_the_job: Takeoff habit: every fixed appliance on the plans gets a line — appliance, rating, circuit, disconnect. If a plan shows the appliance but no circuit home, that is an open question for the packet, not a field surprise. Worked line: a 4,500 W storage water heater at 240 V draws 18.75 A; as a continuous load under 422.13 the circuit is sized at 125 percent — 23.4 A minimum — so the line reads: water heater, 18.75 A, 30 A circuit on 10 AWG copper, lockable disconnect. Every fixed appliance on the plan gets the same four boxes filled before the packet goes out.
sections.figure_idea: Takeoff worksheet strip: appliance, rating, circuit, disconnect — four boxes in a row.
sections.why_it_exists: An appliance is a known, fixed load that runs exactly as hard as its nameplate says, sometimes for hours. A circuit sized by habit instead of by the rating either nuisance-trips under a load that was never a fault, or leaves conductors and terminations carrying more than they were built for. Starting from the marked rating is what keeps both the appliance and the circuit honest.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is protecting an unmarked 16 A appliance with a 20 A breaker 'because it fits.' Section 422.11(E) works the other way: over 13.3 A with no marked maximum, the ceiling is 150 percent of the appliance rating — the breaker follows the appliance, not the other way around. The other common miss is sizing the storage water heater at 100 percent; at 120 gallons or less it is a continuous load at 125 percent (422.13).
inspection_fails: Appliance landed on a circuit sized by habit, not by the appliance's marked rating.
Unmarked appliance over 13.3 A protected above 150 percent of its rating (422.11(E)).
Storage water heater of 120 gallons or less wired at 100 percent instead of 125 percent (422.13).
Fixed appliance on the plans with no circuit assigned — found in the field, not on the takeoff.
Appliance marked with a maximum overcurrent device protected above the marking (422.11).

sections.title: Overcurrent protection for appliances (422.11)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.11 protects the appliance at the size the appliance was built for.
• Where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, that marking governs.
• For a single non-motor appliance fastened in place that is not marked with a maximum OCPD: 20 A maximum if the appliance is rated 13.3 A or less; 150 percent of the rated current maximum if rated over 13.3 A — and where 150 percent does not land on a standard rating, the next higher standard size is permitted (422.11(E)). That 150 percent is a ceiling, not a target.
• Motor-operated appliances follow the motor rules for their protection.
• Infrared heating appliances carry their own subdivision limits in this section.
• 422.11(F): resistance-type heating elements in electric heating appliances rated over 48 A must be subdivided, each subdivided load not over 48 A and protected at not more than 60 A.
sections.on_the_job: Read the appliance label before the breaker is chosen, every time. 'It matched the panel schedule from the last job' is how a 50 A device lands on an appliance marked 30 A maximum. Worked example with no marking: an unmarked fastened-in-place appliance rated 16 A gets 150 percent of 16 A = 24 A; 24 A is not a standard rating, so the next higher standard size, 25 A, is the ceiling. If that appliance were marked 'MAX 30 A,' the label — not the math — would set the breaker.
sections.figure_idea: Appliance label zoom: 'MAX FUSE / BREAKER 30 A' with an arrow to the panel breaker slot.
sections.why_it_exists: An appliance's internal wiring, switches and controls are tested and listed with a specific maximum protective device ahead of them. A larger breaker lets a fault inside the appliance cook its own small conductors long before the breaker trips. The 150 percent allowance exists because some appliances draw starting surges — but it is a ceiling set by the listing, not a size to aim for.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating 150 percent as the required size, or applying it to a marked appliance. When the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs and the percentage math never starts. And where 150 percent lands between standard sizes, only the next higher standard size is permitted — not the next one after that.
inspection_fails: 50 A breaker on an appliance marked 'MAX BREAKER 30 A' — the marking governs, 422.11(E).
Unmarked 16 A appliance protected at 40 A 'to stop nuisance trips' — the ceiling is 150 percent (24 A, next standard size 25 A).
90 A electric heating appliance fed as one load — elements over 48 A must be subdivided, each load not over 48 A, 422.11(F).
Subdivided heating load protected at 80 A — subdivided loads are protected at not more than 60 A, 422.11(F).

sections.title: Storage water heaters — treat the load as continuous for circuit sizing
sections.plain_explanation: Section 422.13 sizes the branch circuit for a fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less at not less than 125 percent of the heater's nameplate rating. In practice that is why a common 4500W, 240V heater (18.75A) lands on a 25A minimum calculation and is conventionally wired on a 30A circuit with 10 AWG copper — the arithmetic must be run for the actual nameplate on the actual job, not copied from the last house. The heater is treated this way because it can run for long stretches recovering a tank.
sections.on_the_job:
Do the division every time: nameplate watts divided by voltage, times 1.25, then choose the standard breaker and conductor that cover it. Write the result on the panel schedule so the next person does not have to reverse-engineer it.

Worked example: a 5,500 W, 240 V heater draws 5,500 ÷ 240 = 22.9 A; × 1.25 = 28.6 A minimum circuit — a 30A breaker on 10 AWG copper covers it. The standard 4,500 W heater works out to 18.75 A × 1.25 = 23.4 A, which is why it also lands on the same 30A / 10 AWG circuit.
sections.why_it_exists: A storage heater does not sip power. After showers or a full tank draw, the elements run flat-out for a long stretch to recover the tank, exactly like a continuous load. A circuit sized at exactly the nameplate amps would run its breaker and terminations at the edge for hours. The 125 percent factor is the continuous-load margin that keeps the circuit cool over those long runs.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing to the nameplate alone: 4,500 W ÷ 240 V = 18.75 A, so a 20 A breaker on 12 AWG. Wrong — 422.13 treats the heater as a continuous load, so the circuit minimum is 18.75 × 1.25 = 23.4 A, and the job lands on a 30 A breaker with 10 AWG copper.

5,500 W heater on a 25 A breaker: below the 28.6 A minimum the 125 percent rule sets.
Circuit copied from the last house without reading the nameplate on the heater actually installed.
Panel schedule shows the heater circuit with no rating recorded — the calc was never run.

sections.title: Cord-and-plug connection for range hoods
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.16(B)(4) lets a listed range hood — and an over-the-range microwave/range hood combination — be cord-and-plug connected instead of hard-wired, but only when every condition in the subsection is met:
• The flexible cord is identified as suitable for use on range hoods in the manufacturer's installation instructions.
• The cord is not less than 18 in. and not over 4 ft long.
• The cord has an equipment grounding conductor and ends in a grounding-type attachment plug. Exception: a listed hood marked as double-insulated does not need the grounding-type plug.
• The receptacle is located so the cord is protected against physical damage.
• The receptacle is accessible.
• The receptacle is supplied by an individual branch circuit.
Cord connection is what lets the hood come down for service without unwiring it. It is a listed, conditioned permission — not a general shortcut for any fixed appliance.
sections.on_the_job: Marion Oaks kitchen: the plan shows an over-the-range microwave/hood combination. Under S-06 it gets its own dedicated 20 A circuit — never shared. The receptacle goes in the cabinet above the unit, where the cord reaches it without crossing the cooktop: the factory cord is 24 in., inside the 18 in. to 4 ft window. Before rough-in, confirm the unit's instructions identify the cord for range hood use; a hood listed for hard-wiring only gets hard-wired, cord kit or not.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma note (company practice, not a 422 rule): the range hood often rides the dishwasher/disposal circuit in Sharma design practice. S-06 still stands on its own — the microwave keeps its own dedicated 20A circuit and is never lumped in with the hood. The wire size on that circuit is PENDING (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA).
sections.why_it_exists: Hoods live over a hot cooktop in grease-laden air, and they come down for cleaning and service more than almost any other fixed appliance. The cord makes that practical. The conditions keep the cord itself from becoming the hazard: short enough to stay off the burners, grounded, protected from damage, and on its own circuit so the hood is not sharing a loaded kitchen circuit.
inspection_fails: Cord-and-plug hood receptacle fed from the small-appliance or dishwasher circuit — not an individual branch circuit.
Hood cord 5 ft long, draped behind the range to reach a receptacle.
Receptacle hidden behind the hood's duct cover — not accessible.
Cord kit added to a hood whose instructions list it for hard-wiring only.
Receptacle located where a cabinet door or the duct pinches the cord.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating cord connection as permission to plug the hood into any handy receptacle — the countertop small-appliance circuit, or the dishwasher/disposal circuit. For a cord-and-plug hood, 422.16(B)(4) requires an individual branch circuit. The other trap is the cord length: over 4 ft fails, even if everything else is right.

sections.title: Disconnecting means for permanently connected appliances
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 422.31 covers how a permanently connected appliance is disconnected for service. Every appliance needs a disconnecting means that opens all ungrounded conductors at once (422.30), and the person servicing the appliance must be able to cut its power and keep it cut. Which device may serve depends on the appliance's rating:
• Not over 300 VA or 1/8 hp — 422.31(A): the branch-circuit switch or circuit breaker may serve as the disconnecting means, where it is within sight from the appliance or is capable of being locked in the open position in compliance with 110.25.
• Over 300 VA or 1/8 hp — 422.31(B): a switch or circuit breaker within sight from the appliance, or capable of being locked in the open position per 110.25, may serve. If the breaker is out of sight and not lockable, provide a disconnect within sight of the appliance.
• Motor-operated appliances over 1/8 hp — 422.31(C): the disconnecting means must be within sight from the appliance, unless a unit switch complying with 422.34 serves as the disconnect.
Within sight means visible and not more than 50 ft away (Article 100). The branch-circuit breaker can serve this role only where the conditions for doing so are met.
sections.on_the_job: At rough-in, decide where each hard-wired appliance's disconnect lives and confirm a servicer can reach it. Florida example: a 4,500 W water heater in the garage on a 30 A circuit. The panel is in the same garage, visible from the water heater and well within 50 ft, so the breaker serves as the disconnect. Put that same water heater on a panel inside the house, out of sight, and the job changes: make the breaker lockable per 110.25 or set a disconnect at the unit. A water heater, an air handler, or a cooktop whose only disconnect is an unlabelled breaker two rooms away is a conversation to have before final, not after.

sections.why_it_exists: Appliances get serviced by someone with the cover off and hands inside — a water heater element swap, an air handler blower. If the only disconnect is a breaker in another room, anyone in the building can turn the unit back on mid-repair. A disconnect within sight of the appliance, or one the servicer can lock open, keeps the person who opened it in control of it.
inspection_fails: Water heater over 300 VA with no disconnect within sight, and the breaker is not capable of being locked open (422.31(B)).
Breaker lockout is a loose clip-on device that does not remain in place with the lock removed (110.25).
Disconnect provided, but it does not open all ungrounded conductors at once (422.30).
Motor-operated appliance over 1/8 hp with no disconnect within sight and no unit switch complying with 422.34 (422.31(C)).
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer: 'the branch-circuit breaker is always the appliance disconnect.' For an appliance over 300 VA whose breaker is out of sight and cannot be locked open, the breaker alone does not comply — 422.31(B) wants a disconnect within sight, or a breaker capable of being locked in the open position per 110.25.

sections.title: Fixed electric space-heating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 424 covers heating that is built into the building: baseboard heaters, wall heaters, radiant panels and cables, duct heaters, and boilers used for space heat. Three ideas run the article:
• Heating is a continuous load. Branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load on the circuit (424.4(B)) — a heater runs for hours at full draw; it is not a convenience load that happens to get warm.
• The equipment must be listed and installed to its instructions (110.3(B)).
• Disconnects and controls must let the heater be serviced and shut off safely. The 424.19 disconnect kills the heater, its controller and any supplementary overcurrent devices in one operation, is lockable in the open position, and is rated at least 125 percent of the load it switches.
Circuits supplying two or more heater outlets are rated 15, 20, 25 or 30 A; fixed infrared heating in other than dwelling units may go to 50 A (424.4(A)). In Florida houses Sharma meets this article most often at duct heat strips in an air handler and at the occasional wall or bath heater.
sections.on_the_job: A Sharma new-construction home in Ocala gets a 3-ton air handler with a 10 kW strip kit. The strip nameplate reads 10 kW at 240 V, which is 41.7 A. Treat it as continuous: 41.7 × 1.25 = 52.1 A, so the circuit lands on a 60 A breaker with 6 AWG copper. Confirm the disconnect and control arrangement before the air handler is set: the switch at the unit must kill the strips, the blower and the supplementary fuses together, and lock open. Heat strips are also a load-calc input — tell the office the strip size you actually installed, not the one the plan first showed.

nec2023_change.change: New 424.48 allows heating cable in, on or behind walls if the cable is identified for walls, has GFCI, AFCI and a grounding means, and stays at or below 4 ft. Effective January 1, 2026. Heating cable can now go in, on or behind a wall when the cable or cable set is identified for wall use.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 424.48 Heating cable in walls

sections.why_it_exists: A heater does not cycle like a receptacle load — on a cold morning it pulls full nameplate current for hours. Sizing at 100 percent runs conductors and breakers at their limit until something fails, so the article builds the 125 percent margin in. The one-operation disconnect exists because a strip heater with a live blower, or a second live element, is exactly how a service tech gets burned or shocked inside an air handler.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the heater circuit at 100 percent because 'resistance heat is a simple load.' Fixed electric space heat is a continuous load: conductors and overcurrent protection go at 125 percent of the nameplate. A 41.7 A strip on a 50 A breaker is the wrong answer — it needs 52.1 A of capacity before you pick the device.
inspection_fails: Heater circuit sized at 100 percent of nameplate — no 125 percent continuous factor (424.4(B)).
Air-handler disconnect kills the heat strips but leaves the blower and controller live (424.19).
Disconnect cannot be locked in the open position while the heater is serviced (424.19, 110.25).
Heater installed against its listing instructions — clearances to combustibles not kept (110.3(B)).

sections.title: Branch circuits for fixed electric space heating (424.4(A), 424.4(B))
sections.plain_explanation:
Fixed electric space heating — baseboard, wall heaters, ceiling heat, and the electric heat built into equipment — is served by individual branch circuits under 424.4(A), with the central systems the article names as the exception pattern.
• 424.4(B): the heating load is treated as continuous. Branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load on the circuit, before any other load is considered.
• Circuits supplying two or more heater outlets are rated 15, 20, 25 or 30 A.
• In other than dwelling units, fixed infrared heating may be on circuits up to 50 A (424.4(A)).
• (424.3(A)/(B) are the 2017 numbers for these rules.)
A heater is not a convenience load that happens to get warm; it runs for hours at full draw.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: a 4,800 W, 240 V wall heater draws 20 A (4,800 ÷ 240). Continuous sizing makes the circuit 20 × 1.25 = 25 A — so the circuit is built at 25 A or above, never the 20 A circuit the raw math suggests. Same math in a Florida bonus room: two 1,500 W baseboards on one circuit draw 3,000 W ÷ 240 V = 12.5 A, and 12.5 × 1.25 = 15.6 A, so that circuit is 20 A, not 15 A.
sections.figure_idea: One heater, two math lines: nameplate amps, then the 125 percent continuous line landing on the breaker size.
sections.why_it_exists: On a cold night a space heater does not cycle — it sits at full current for hours. Conductors and a breaker sized at exactly the load would run at their thermal limit the whole time, aging terminations and inviting nuisance trips. The 125 percent continuous factor keeps every part of the circuit below its rating during the longest run the heater can make.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the heater circuit at nameplate amps: 20 A heater, 20 A breaker, done. 424.4(B) treats the load as continuous, so the exam answer is 25 A. The second trap is the section number — in a 2017 book these rules sit at 424.3; in the 2020 book they are at 424.4.
inspection_fails: 4,800 W wall heater on a 20 A circuit — heating load not sized at 125 percent, 424.4(B).
Two baseboard heaters sharing a general lighting circuit instead of an individual branch circuit, 424.4(A).
40 A circuit feeding three heater outlets — circuits for two or more heater outlets stop at 30 A, 424.4(A).
Fixed infrared heaters in a shop on a 60 A circuit — outside dwelling units the cap is 50 A, 424.4(A).

sections.title: Branch-circuit sizing for fixed space heat — 125 percent
sections.plain_explanation: Section 424.4(B) is where this rule lives in the 2020 edition — it was 424.3(B) in 2017, before the Article 424 reorganization. The 2020 text states the sizing directly instead of using the old 'shall be considered continuous load' sentence: the branch-circuit conductors for fixed electric space-heating equipment and any associated motors shall be sized not smaller than 125 percent of the load. Overcurrent protection is sized at the same 125 percent through the continuous-load rules of 210.19(A)(1) and 210.20(A), so in practice both the conductors and the breaker come out at 125 percent of the total load connected to the circuit, heater plus any blower or fan motor in the same equipment.
sections.on_the_job:
Run the math at 125 percent: total nameplate amps, heater plus motor, times 1.25 — then select the conductor and the breaker.

Worked example: a 10 kW duct heater at 240 V draws 41.7 A; × 1.25 = 52.1 A — conductors rated at least 52.1 A (6 AWG copper at the 75°C column gives 65 A) on a 60A breaker, and the blower motor amps in the same equipment are added to the heater amps before the 125 percent is applied.

Same math with the air handler's blower in the calc: heater 41.7 A plus a 6 A blower motor is 47.7 A connected; × 1.25 = 59.6 A — still a 60A breaker, and the 6 AWG copper still covers it. Leave the motor out and the paperwork says 52.1 A for a circuit that really carries more.
sections.why_it_exists: Electric space heat is the classic continuous load: on the coldest night the strips run for hours without cycling off. Conductors and a breaker sized at exactly the load amps would sit at their thermal edge all night, heating terminations and inviting nuisance trips that leave the house cold. The 125 percent factor is the margin that keeps a long, full-load run safe.
sections.exam_trap: Two traps live here. First, hunting for the rule under its 2017 address, 424.3(B) — in the 2020 book it is 424.4(B). Second, applying 125 percent to the heater nameplate and forgetting the blower motor in the same equipment: the motor amps are added first, then the whole total is multiplied.

Blower motor amps left out of the calc; conductors and breaker sized on the strips alone.
8 AWG copper (50 A at 75°C) on a heat load that calculates to a 52.1 A minimum.
Breaker bumped up for the 125 percent but the conductors left at the old size.
