sections.title: Disconnecting means for fixed space-heating equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 424.19 requires a disconnecting means for fixed electric space-heating equipment — baseboard and wall heaters, duct heaters, and heat strips in an air handler. One operation has to kill the whole machine:
• The disconnect must simultaneously disconnect the heater, the motor controller(s) and any supplementary overcurrent protective device(s) from all ungrounded conductors.
• It must be lockable in the open position under 110.25 — the locking provision is part of the switch or breaker and stays in place with or without the lock.
• The disconnect must have an ampere rating not less than 125 percent of the total load of the motors and the heaters.
• Equipment with supplementary overcurrent protection: the disconnect is within sight from those devices — visible and not more than 50 ft away.
• Equipment without supplementary overcurrent protection: the branch-circuit switch or breaker may serve as the disconnect, if it is within sight from the heater or lockable under 110.25 [424.19(B)].
• A unit switch that is part of the equipment, with a marked "off" position, may serve as the disconnect where it disconnects all ungrounded conductors [424.19(C)].
A duct heater in an air handler is normally disconnected at the air handler's disconnect — the 440/424 boundary matters on a change-out, because the strips and the blower are one piece of equipment at service time.
sections.on_the_job: Air-handler change-out in a Florida garage: the new unit carries 10 kW of strip heat and a blower, fed as one piece of equipment. The disconnect at the air handler must kill the strips, the blower and the controller together — test all three dead before your hands go in. The strip circuit is sized at 125 percent under 424.4(B): 10 kW at 240 V is 41.7 A — 52.1 A minimum, 60 A breaker. If you move the disconnect on the change-out, re-verify at the new location that it still opens the whole unit, and check the heat-strip circuit before start-up. Keep the disconnect within reach of the person servicing the unit.
sections.why_it_exists: Heat strips and a blower share one cabinet, and the tech services them with the cabinet open and both hands inside. If the switch he opened kills the strips but leaves the blower or the controls live — or someone resets a breaker down the hall mid-repair — the "dead" unit starts or bites. One disconnect that opens everything and locks open is what makes the equipment safe to open up.
inspection_fails: Disconnect opens the heat strips but the blower and controls stay live — it must open the heater, the controller and the supplementary protection together.
Out-of-sight disconnect with no lockable provision, or a portable hasp clipped on — 110.25 requires the provision to stay in place with or without the lock.
Unit has supplementary fuses inside, and the disconnect is around the corner, out of sight from those devices.
Unit switch used as the disconnect with no marked "off" position, or it opens only one ungrounded conductor.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is "the panel breaker is the disconnect, full stop." That only works for equipment without supplementary overcurrent protection, and only when the breaker is within sight of the heater or lockable under 110.25. If the unit carries its own supplementary fuses or breakers, the disconnect must be within sight from those devices.

sections.title: Fixed resistance and electrode industrial process heating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 425 covers electric heating used for an industrial process rather than for comfort: process tanks, ovens, and similar equipment.
• The article follows the use, not the hardware: the same heating element is 424 work when it warms people and 425 work when it heats a product.
• Sharma's residential and light commercial work rarely installs it, so this page is the article's scope page.
• Where a commercial job includes process heat, work the article with the equipment listing, and ask Mike before treating it like space heat under 424.
sections.on_the_job: Do not borrow 424 rules for a 425 load by habit. Identify the article from the equipment's use, then apply that article plus the listing. Example: a small commercial job adds an electric process tank heater. Before quoting, get the nameplate and the listing instructions, confirm which article the job falls under, and let Mike review the plan: the wire and protection follow 425 and the listing, not the duct-heater job from last week.

sections.why_it_exists: Process heaters run unattended for long cycles, often around water, chemicals and product that cannot tolerate a fault. The article exists because a tank or an oven is not a baseboard heater: its controls, disconnects and protection follow the process and the listing, not comfort-heating habits carried over from 424.

sections.title: Fixed outdoor electric deicing and snow-melting equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 426 covers fixed electric equipment installed outdoors to melt snow and ice: heating cable and panels in pavements, walks, driveways, roofs and gutters. It is a later-pass article for a Florida book — Sharma does not install snow-melting in its territory — and it is included here so Chapter 4 walks the NEC in complete official order. The rules that do the work when this equipment appears:
• Continuous load (426.4): branch-circuit conductors and the overcurrent device are sized at not less than 125 percent of the total heater load.
• Ground-fault protection of equipment (426.28): GFPE must be provided for the equipment, except for mineral-insulated, metal-sheathed cable embedded in a noncombustible medium. GFPE protects equipment — it is not a personnel GFCI.
• Disconnecting means (426.50): a means that disconnects all ungrounded conductors at the same time, capable of being locked open.
• Identification (426.13): the presence of a deicing or snow-melting installation must be indicated, so nobody cores or cuts into a heated slab blind.
sections.on_the_job: If a Florida job somehow specifies deicing equipment — a northern builder's standard detail copied onto a Florida plan is the usual way — flag it to the office rather than installing or deleting it silently. If the office ever approves one, the math looks like this: a 2,400 W heated walk on 240 V draws 10 A; treated as the continuous load it is, the circuit sizes at 125 percent, 12.5 A, so a 15 A breaker is the smallest standard pick — and it must be a GFPE breaker, not a standard one (426.28).
sections.florida_note: Florida note: no snow load in Sharma's territory; treat any 426 equipment on a Florida plan as a probable copy-over from another climate and confirm with the builder.

sections.why_it_exists: Heating cable lives buried in concrete and asphalt, where a nicked cable or failed splice leaks current into wet, grounded pavement. That leakage is far too small to trip a breaker, but it can sputter and arc inside the slab until something catches — which is why 426.28 puts ground-fault protection of equipment on the circuit. The 125 percent sizing exists because the load runs for hours in the coldest weather: conductors and breakers sized at exactly 100 percent would cook at their terminals.

Heater circuit sized at 100 percent of load; deicing is a continuous load, 125 percent (426.4).
Disconnect opens only one ungrounded conductor, or cannot be locked open (426.50).
Heated slab not identified at the panel or on the plans (426.13).

sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating GFPE and GFCI as the same device. A personnel GFCI trips at 4–6 mA and can nuisance-trip on a long heating-cable run; the ground-fault protection of equipment that 426.28 requires typically trips around 30 mA (manufacturers vary) and exists to keep a damaged cable from arcing inside the slab. The reverse trap is skipping ground-fault protection entirely because 'nobody touches a slab' — the protection is for the equipment, not for people.

sections.title: Fixed electric heating equipment for pipelines and vessels — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 427 covers fixed electric heating equipment for pipelines and vessels: heat-tracing cable and heating panels that keep a pipe from freezing or hold a process fluid at temperature.
• Scope: the heating cable or panel, its controls and its branch circuit (427.1).
• The load is continuous: branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load (427.4).
• Ground-fault protection of equipment is required on the branch circuits that supply heat tracing and heating panels (427.22). It is equipment protection, commonly a 30 mA trip — not a 4–6 mA personnel GFCI. A narrow exception covers industrial plants with alarm indication and qualified maintenance.
• Heating cables carry a grounded conductive covering: the metal braid or jacket is the fault path that lets the protection see a failure (427.23).
• Caution signs or markings go on the pipe or vessel at intervals of not more than 20 ft, and next to equipment that gets serviced (427.13).
• Each installation has a disconnecting means that opens all ungrounded conductors (427.55(A)).
Sharma meets this article as pipe heat trace on exposed commercial plumbing and in freeze protection details, not in ordinary house work.
sections.on_the_job: A small commercial building in Ocala has 40 ft of exposed domestic water pipe and a backflow preventer in an unconditioned meter room. Sharma installs self-regulating heat trace under the pipe insulation, fed from a 20 A GFPE breaker — Sharma's commercial minimum branch circuit is 20 A. The cable load is 8 A; figured as a continuous load at 125 percent, that is 10 A, well inside the circuit. Caution markings go on the pipe at 20 ft intervals and at the valve that gets serviced. Install the heat trace exactly to its listing: correct cable for the pipe, correct controller and sensor location, GFPE in place and tested. Photograph the controller setting at turnover.

nec2023_change.change: Section 427.35, which covered the installation of line frequency induction heating equipment and accessories for pipelines and vessels, was deleted.
nec2023_change.source: Carosella/NFPA-based 2023 NEC change workbook: 427.35 Scope

sections.why_it_exists: A heat-trace cable lives outdoors, under insulation, wrapped on a pipe full of water. When its insulation fails, the fault can arc and sputter without ever drawing enough current to trip a plain breaker — heating the pipe covering instead. GFPE watches for that small leak to ground and opens the circuit, and the grounded braid gives the fault a path the protection can see. The caution signs warn the next trade off a live cable hidden under insulation.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for a Class A GFCI. Section 427.22 asks for ground-fault protection of equipment, which trips around 30 mA to catch a failing cable; a 4–6 mA personnel GFCI is a different device that nuisance-trips on long runs. Second trap: sizing the branch circuit at 100 percent of the cable load — heating is a continuous load and takes 125 percent (427.4).
inspection_fails: Heat-trace branch circuit with no ground-fault protection of equipment (427.22).
No caution signs or markings along the heated pipe, so the next crew buries a live cable under insulation with no warning (427.13).
Cable installed without its grounded conductive covering, or the braid left ungrounded at the termination (427.23).
Branch circuit sized at 100 percent of the heating load — a continuous load takes 125 percent (427.4).
Controller sensor hanging in the air instead of strapped to the pipe, so the cable cooks the covering or the pipe freezes.

sections.title: Motors, motor circuits, and controllers — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 430 is the longest working article in Chapter 4 and the one most often misapplied, because it is a system, not a single rule. Five jobs, five sizing bases:
• Conductors — from table full-load current, at 125 percent for a continuous-duty motor (430.22).
• Overload protection — separate from the breaker, sized from the nameplate current of the motor actually installed: 125 percent for a motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 or greater, or a marked temperature rise of 40 °C or less; 115 percent for all other motors (430.32).
• Short-circuit and ground-fault protection — from the Table 430.52 percentages of table FLC: an inverse-time breaker may go to 250 percent, which is why a motor breaker can look oversized for its wire.
• A controller rated for the motor.
• A disconnect within sight (430.102), rated at least 115 percent of table FLC or by its horsepower rating (430.110).
430.6 is the traffic rule behind all of it: everything except the overloads starts from the Article 430 tables, because the next replacement motor may differ from this nameplate. Using one number for all five jobs is the classic 430 error. Air-conditioning equipment is pulled out of parts of 430 by Article 440, which has its own nameplate-driven rules — always check which article governs the equipment in front of you.
sections.on_the_job: Work a motor in this order, every time: (1) table FLC for conductors and short-circuit protection, (2) nameplate FLA for overloads, (3) disconnect within sight, (4) controller rating. Write all four down before you order material. Example: a 10 hp, 208 V three-phase motor has a table FLC of 30.8 A. Its conductors need 125 percent — 38.5 A of ampacity. The inverse-time breaker may go to 250 percent — 77 A — which is why it looks oversized next to the wire; the overloads, set from the nameplate, are the protection that actually watches the load.

nec2023_change.change: Rebuilt motors now have a home in 430.2: they're allowed when the work follows the manufacturer's instructions, or a nationally recognized standard if the maker offers none. A reconditioned motor can go back into service when the rebuild followed the manufacturer's instructions.
nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 430.2 Reconditioned motors

sections.why_it_exists: A motor draws several times its running current at start-up, and it can sit stalled and cooking without ever tripping protection sized for ordinary loads. Article 430 splits the protection into separate jobs so starting current can pass, a stalled motor still gets cleared, and the overload device — not the big breaker — watches the motor and its conductors against a slow overload.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is one number for the whole job — usually the nameplate FLA, used for the conductors, the breaker, the overloads and the disconnect. Only the overloads come off the nameplate. Conductors, short-circuit protection and the disconnect all start from table full-load current under 430.6, because a replacement motor may not match this one's nameplate.

No disconnect within sight of the motor (430.102).

sections.title: Which current do you size from — table values vs. nameplate
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.6 is the traffic rule for the whole article. For sizing conductors, disconnects, controllers, and short-circuit/ground-fault protection, you use the full-load current values from the Article 430 tables for the motor's horsepower and voltage — not the amps printed on that particular motor's nameplate, because the next replacement motor may differ. Overload protection is the exception: it is sized from the actual nameplate current of the motor installed, because it protects that specific machine. Mixing those two bases up is the single most common motor calculation error.

The fuller table is on the 430.250 page. If the horsepower and voltage in front of you are not listed here, pull the value from the printed table for that combination — do not scale from a nearby row.
sections.on_the_job: A Sharma crew replaces a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase air compressor motor in a Lakeland shop. Table 430.248 gives 28 A for that motor, so the conductors, disconnect, and short-circuit protection are all figured from 28 A — the conductors at 125 percent of it under 430.22. The new motor's nameplate reads 26 A, and that number goes only on the overload line of the worksheet. If the nameplate had read 30 A, the overloads would follow 30 A — but the conductors would still be sized from the 28 A table value.
sections.why_it_exists: Motors of the same horsepower are not identical — one maker's 5 hp motor draws more than another's. If conductors were sized from one motor's nameplate, the replacement motor installed ten years later could overload them. The tables give one standard current for each horsepower and voltage, so the wiring outlasts any single machine. Overload protection is the opposite case: it guards the motor actually bolted down, so it follows that motor's nameplate.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is using the nameplate for everything because it is the motor in front of you. Nameplate current sizes only the overload protection. Conductors, disconnects, controllers, and short-circuit and ground-fault protection all come from the Article 430 tables — Table 430.248 for single-phase, Table 430.250 for three-phase.
inspection_fails: Motor branch-circuit conductors sized from the nameplate current, below the table value — 430.6(A).
Overload protection sized from the table value instead of the installed motor's nameplate current.
Replacement motor installed on conductors that were sized to the old motor's lower nameplate amps.

sections.title: Conductors for a single motor — 125 percent of table full-load current
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.22 sizes the branch-circuit conductors feeding one continuous-duty motor at not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables.
• Start from the table FLC for the horsepower and voltage — Table 430.248 for single-phase motors — not from the nameplate amps.
• Multiply by 1.25, then select the conductor from the ampacity table using the temperature column the terminations allow.
• Intermittent and short-time duty motors are treated under their own parts of this section, so the duty rating on the nameplate decides which rule you are in before you do any arithmetic.
The extra quarter covers the heating of a motor that runs for long periods at full load.
sections.on_the_job:
Take the table FLC for the horsepower and voltage, multiply by 1.25, then select the conductor from the ampacity table using the correct temperature column for the terminations. Do not size the wire from the nameplate amps and do not round the 125 percent away.

Worked example, a shop compressor in Marion County: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase motor has a table FLC of 28 A (Table 430.248). Conductors: 28 × 1.25 = 35 A minimum — 10 AWG copper at the 75 °C column (35 A) is the smallest conductor that covers it, before any voltage-drop or adjustment checks.
sections.why_it_exists: A continuous-duty motor can sit at full load for hours — a well pump on a dry day, a shop compressor on a busy one. Conductors sized at exactly full-load current would run at their ampacity limit the whole time, with no margin for a hot attic or a tight bundle. The 125 percent factor is thermal headroom, so the wire never becomes the weak point in the circuit.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reading the amps off the motor nameplate and sizing the conductors to that number. 430.22 wants the table full-load current times 125 percent. The nameplate current is what the overload protection is set from — it is not the conductor number.
inspection_fails: Motor conductors sized from nameplate amps instead of the Article 430 table FLC, 430.22.
5 hp, 230 V motor wired with 12 AWG copper (25 A at 75 °C) — 125 percent of the 28 A table FLC is 35 A.
125 percent factor dropped because 'the motor never runs that long' — continuous-duty sizing is not optional, 430.22.
Conductor picked from the 90 °C column where the equipment terminations are rated 75 °C.

page_quiz.explain_plain: Table 310.16, 75 °C column: 10 AWG copper is 35 A; 12 AWG copper is 25 A and 10 AWG aluminum is 30 A.

sections.title: Conductors feeding several motors
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.24 sizes conductors that feed two or more motors (or motors with other loads):
• Take 125 percent of the full-load current of the largest motor.
• Add the full-load currents of the other motors at 100 percent.
• Add any other loads under their own rules.
All full-load currents come from the Article 430 tables — Table 430.248 for single-phase, Table 430.250 for three-phase — not from nameplates (430.6). The largest motor gets the continuous-duty margin; the rest are added at face value, on the reasonable basis that the feeder sees the sum. It is the feeder-level companion to the single-motor rule in 430.22.
sections.on_the_job: Small Orlando shop, one feeder for three 230 V single-phase motors: a 5 hp compressor at 28 A table FLC, a 3 hp at 17 A, and a 2 hp at 12 A. Largest first at 125 percent: 28 × 1.25 = 35 A. Add the rest at face value: 35 + 17 + 12 = 64 A minimum conductor ampacity. A 6 AWG copper conductor in the 75°C column is rated 65 A (Table 310.16), so it covers the feeder before any adjustment or correction factors. Build the sum in a labelled column — largest motor first at 125 percent, then each additional motor at 100 percent — so the next person can audit it. Do not apply 125 percent to every motor on the feeder, and do not size a multi-motor feeder from one nameplate.

sections.why_it_exists: The feeder carries every motor at once, in one raceway, where heat has nowhere to go. The largest motor is the one most likely to run loaded for hours at a stretch, so it carries the continuous-duty margin. Size the feeder at a flat 100 percent of the sum and it runs hot on exactly those long runs — insulation ages in the conduit where nobody sees it.
inspection_fails: Feeder conductors sized at 100 percent of the sum of motor FLCs — no 125 percent factor on the largest motor (430.24).
Motor feeder sized from a nameplate current instead of the Article 430 table values (430.6).
Non-motor load on the same feeder left out of the conductor calculation.
Feeder calculation missing from the job paperwork — the conductor size cannot be audited.
sections.exam_trap: Two trap answers: applying 125 percent to every motor on the feeder — only the largest gets the margin — and sizing from the largest motor's nameplate amps. Section 430.24 runs on table full-load currents under 430.6, with the 125 percent factor on the largest motor only.

page_quiz.question: Under 430.24, which motor is taken at 125 percent?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Only the largest motor gets the continuous-duty margin; the others are added at 100 percent of their table FLC.

page_quiz.question: Motors of 28 A, 17 A and 12 A table FLC share a feeder. Minimum conductor ampacity?
page_quiz.explain_plain: Largest at 125 percent: 28 × 1.25 = 35. The rest at face value: 35 + 17 + 12 = 64 A.

page_quiz.question: Which current do you use for each motor in the 430.24 sum?
choices: The nameplate amps of the motor installed
The Article 430 table FLC for the horsepower and voltage
The breaker size on each branch circuit
page_quiz.explain_plain: 430.6 sends conductor and protection sizing to the Article 430 tables, not the nameplate; the nameplate is for overload protection.

sections.title: Overload protection — protects the motor from running too hot
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.32 requires overload protection for continuous-duty motors over the small sizes the article sets. Size it from the motor's nameplate full-load current — the actual machine in front of you — with the percentage set by the motor's service factor and temperature-rise markings. The overload device watches running current over time and trips before the windings cook; it is not there to clear a short circuit, which is the branch protective device's job. A motor with built-in thermal protection meets this requirement through its own device where the article allows it.
The percentages in 430.32(A)(1), applied to the nameplate full-load current:
• Motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 or greater — 125 percent
• Motor with a marked temperature rise of 40 °C or less — 125 percent
• All other motors — 115 percent
If an overload selected at those percentages will not let the motor start or carry its load, 430.32(C) permits stepping up — to not more than 140 percent for the first two cases, 130 percent for all others. The step-up is a documented exception for a motor that will not run, not the starting point for selection.
sections.on_the_job: Read service factor and rise off the nameplate before you select or set an overload. Worked example: a 3 hp, 230 V pool pump on a Marion Oaks job — the tables give 17 A for that horsepower, but the overload comes off the plate: nameplate FLA 15.2 A, service factor marked 1.15, so 15.2 × 125% = 19.0 A, and the overload is set at 19 A. If the overload trips repeatedly, measure the running amps and find the mechanical cause — a failing bearing, a clogged pump basket, low voltage — do not solve a tripping overload by setting it higher than 430.32 permits.

No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.

sections.why_it_exists: A motor rarely fails at a dead short; it fails cooking slowly at 120 or 130 percent of rating, hour after hour, until the insulation gives up. The breaker cannot see that — it is sized to ride through starting current. The overload is the one device watching the motor's own heat, which is why it is set from that motor's nameplate and not from a table.
inspection_fails: Overload set from the Table 430.250 value instead of the installed motor's nameplate FLA.
Overload cranked past the 430.32(C) ceiling to stop nuisance trips, with no mechanical cause found.
No overload protection at all on a continuous-duty motor — a breaker alone does not do this job.
Overload sized at 125% on a motor with no service factor or rise marking that qualifies for it — 115% is the pick.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the overload from the Article 430 tables, the way conductors and disconnects are sized. Tables are for everything except the overload: 430.32 works off the nameplate FLA of the installed motor, because the overload protects that specific machine. The second trap is starting at the 430.32(C) step-up percentages — 140 and 130 percent are the ceiling for a motor that will not run at the first selection, not the selection.

sections.title: Branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for motors
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.52 sizes the device that clears a fault on a motor branch circuit, using the percentages in Table 430.52 applied to the table full-load current. The device type decides which percentage applies. These percentages are deliberately far above running current, because the device must ride through motor starting inrush without opening, while still clearing a fault. That is why a motor circuit can legally have a breaker that looks oversized for its wire — the overload device, not the breaker, protects the motor and, through its sizing rules, the circuit against overload.
• Worked example: the 5 hp, 230 V motor at 28 A table FLC takes an inverse-time breaker of at most 28 × 2.50 = 70 A.
• If that device will not hold through starting, 430.52(C)(1) Exception No. 2(c) permits an inverse-time breaker up to 400 percent where the FLC is 100 A or less — an exception to document, not a habit.
• Exception No. 1 is the next-higher-standard-size permission, for where the table percentage does not land on a standard rating.
• Instantaneous-trip breakers: 430.52(C)(3) Exception No. 1 permits up to 1300 percent where the 800 percent setting won't let the motor start; Design B energy-efficient premium motors may go up to 1700 percent.
sections.on_the_job: Never judge a motor circuit by house-circuit instincts. Check all three together: conductor at 125 percent of table FLC (430.22), overload from the nameplate (430.32), fault protection from Table 430.52. If one of the three is missing from the job paperwork, the calculation is not finished. On a Sharma pump or air-handler swap, that three-line check goes on the work order before the old disconnect is reused.
sections.why_it_exists: A motor draws several times its running current for the first seconds of every start. A device sized like a house-circuit breaker would trip on every start, so the fault device is set high and has one job: clear short circuits and ground faults fast. Running protection is a separate job, given to the overload device.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer downsizes the breaker to match the wire — 'a 70 A breaker on wire sized for 35 A is a violation.' On a motor branch circuit it is not: Table 430.52 allows an inverse-time breaker up to 250 percent of table FLC, and the overload device provides the running protection. The violation is the reverse — a fault device above the table percentage with no exception behind it.
inspection_fails: Inverse-time breaker above 250% of table FLC with no documented exception (Table 430.52).
Breaker swapped larger after nuisance trips, with no check of the Table 430.52 ceiling.
Overload protection missing, or set from the table FLC instead of the motor nameplate (430.32).
Conductors under 125% of table FLC feeding the motor (430.22).

tables.note: Instantaneous-trip: 1100% for Design B energy-efficient motors; up to 1300% (1700% for Design B energy-efficient premium motors) under 430.52(C)(3) Exception No. 1 where the motor will not start.

figures.alt: Bar chart of the Table 430.52 maximum ratings as a percentage of table full-load current — inverse-time breaker 250 percent, dual-element fuse 175 percent, nontime-delay fuse 300 percent, instantaneous-trip breaker 800 percent — with a worked example: 28 amperes table FLC takes a 70 ampere inverse-time breaker.

sections.title: Feeder protection where several motors share a feeder (430.62)
sections.plain_explanation:
When one feeder supplies several motor branch circuits, 430.62(A) caps the feeder's protective device:
• No larger than the largest branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault device on the feeder,
• plus the full-load currents of the other motors on that feeder.
The feeder conductors themselves are sized under 430.24 — 125 percent of the largest motor plus 100 percent of the rest. The two rules work as a pair: the wire math keeps the feeder from running hot, and the device math keeps a fault on one motor from being invisible to a feeder breaker sized for everything at once. The 430.62 result is a ceiling, not a target — a smaller standard device is always permitted.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: three motors at 14 A, 10 A, and 10 A table FLC, largest branch device 40 A. Feeder device ceiling: 40 + 10 + 10 = 60 A — a 60 A feeder breaker is the largest permitted, and anything bigger is a violation even if the conductors could carry it. Feeder conductors, by the other formula: 14 × 1.25 + 10 + 10 = 37.5 A minimum ampacity before other adjustments. Write both numbers on the panel schedule; they come from different sections and answer different questions.
sections.figure_idea: Feeder tree: three motor branches joining one feeder, the two formulas written on the feeder segment.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: If the feeder breaker is sized like a service — big enough for every motor's starting surge added together — a fault on the smallest motor may never draw enough current to open it, and the fault burns until something else gives. Capping the feeder device at the largest branch device plus the other motors' running currents keeps it close enough to see a branch fault, while the branch devices and the motors' overloads do their own jobs.
inspection_fails: Feeder breaker larger than the 430.62(A) ceiling — largest branch device plus the other motors' FLC.
Feeder protective device sized with the 430.24 conductor formula (125 percent of the largest motor).
Feeder conductors sized with the device formula — no 125 percent factor on the largest motor (430.24).
Largest branch-circuit device upsized without rechecking the feeder device ceiling.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answers swap the pair: sizing the feeder device with the 430.24 conductor formula, or sizing the conductors with the 430.62 device formula. The device ceiling is the largest branch device plus the other motors' full-load currents — there is no 125 percent factor anywhere in it.

sections.title: The motor disconnect must be within sight
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.102 places the disconnecting means for a motor and its controller within sight from the equipment it disconnects. 'In sight' is the Article 100 meaning: visible, and not more than 50 ft away.
• Stand at the motor: you must be able to see its disconnect.
• Where the disconnect cannot be within sight, it must be capable of being locked in the open position under the conditions the article allows.
A breaker in a panel across the building, with no lockable arrangement, does not give a servicer control of the machine in front of them.
sections.on_the_job: Stand at the motor and point at its disconnect before you call the job done. If you cannot see it, either move it, add the local disconnect, or confirm the lockable arrangement the article permits and document it. On a Sharma service call at a Kissimmee house, the air-handler blower's only disconnect was the breaker in the garage panel — about 70 ft away and around two corners. That fails the within-sight test, so a local disconnect went in 8 ft from the air handler, in plain view of anyone working on it. The same within-sight habit is what 440.14 demands for HVAC equipment.
sections.why_it_exists: The person servicing a motor has to know the machine cannot be re-energized behind their back. A disconnect you can see is a disconnect you control: nobody restarts the equipment without walking into your line of sight. Where sight is impossible, a lock in the open position is the substitute — your lock, your key, your machine.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'in the same room' or 'on the same floor.' Within sight is a defined term with two parts: the disconnect must be visible AND not more than 50 ft away. A labeled breaker in a panel 80 ft down the hall fails both the exam question and the rule, unless it can be locked open as the article allows.
inspection_fails: Motor disconnect in a remote panel — not within sight and not lockable (430.102).
Disconnect visible from the motor but more than 50 ft away.
Sight line blocked — stored material between the motor and its disconnect.
No disconnect within sight of the condenser unit (440.14).

sections.title: What may serve as the motor disconnect
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.109 lists the types of switches and devices permitted to serve as a motor disconnect. The general list at 430.109(A):
• A listed motor-circuit switch rated in horsepower
• A listed molded case circuit breaker
• A listed molded case switch
• An instantaneous-trip breaker that is part of a listed combination controller, or a listed self-protected combination controller
• A listed manual motor controller additionally marked 'Suitable as Motor Disconnect,' installed between the final branch-circuit protective device and the motor
Small motors get their own paths. For stationary motors of 1/8 horsepower or less, the branch-circuit overcurrent device may serve as the disconnect (430.109(B)), and cord-and-plug arrangements for small motors sit with 430.111. For stationary motors of 2 horsepower or less and 300 volts or less, a general-use switch rated at not less than twice the motor full-load current is permitted, as is an AC general-use snap switch where the motor current is not more than 80 percent of the switch rating (430.109(C)). A general-use switch that is fine for a lighting load is not automatically a motor disconnect; the device must be rated for interrupting a motor circuit of that horsepower.
sections.on_the_job: Read the horsepower rating on the switch, not just the amp rating, before you land a motor on it. When the disconnect is a breaker in a panelboard, confirm it is a permitted type for that motor and that the within-sight rule in 430.102 is separately satisfied. Small-motor case: a 1/2 hp, 115 V exhaust fan motor has a table full-load current of 9.8 A (Table 430.248). On the 430.109(C) path, a general-use switch rated at least twice that — 19.6 A — serves as the disconnect, so a 20 A switch is the pick; a 15 A lighting toggle is not, whatever is on the truck.
sections.why_it_exists: A motor is not a light bulb. Starting current runs several times the running current, and opening a loaded motor circuit draws an arc the device has to survive thousands of times. A switch chosen by amps alone can weld its contacts or fail closed, leaving a servicer working on a machine that is still alive. The horsepower rating is the proof the device was tested to make and break motor current.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is 'a 20 A switch for a 20 A motor circuit.' Section 430.109 is a type list, not an amp list: outside the small-motor paths, the disconnect must be a horsepower-rated device or another listed type the section names. The companion trap is forgetting that type is only half the check — 430.110 still sizes the disconnect at not less than 115 percent of the table full-load current, and 430.102 still wants it within sight.
inspection_fails: General-use lighting switch installed as the disconnect for a motor over the small-motor limits, with no horsepower rating.
Manual motor controller used as the disconnect without the 'Suitable as Motor Disconnect' marking (430.109(A)(6)).
Disconnect sized under 115 percent of the motor's table full-load current (430.110).
Permitted device type, but the disconnect is not within sight of the motor (430.102).
General-use switch under twice the full-load current on a 2 hp or less stationary motor (430.109(C)(1)).

sections.title: Rating of the motor disconnect — at least 115 percent
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.110 sizes the disconnecting means for a motor circuit:
• A general-use switch used as a motor disconnect must have an ampere rating of at least 115 percent of the motor's full-load current, taken from the Article 430 tables — not the nameplate (430.6).
• Horsepower-rated devices are selected by their horsepower rating for the motor served.
The disconnect is a switching device that must safely make and break motor current, which is why its sizing basis is its own rule and not simply 'match the breaker.' Worked check: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase motor has a table full-load current of 28 A. 115 percent of 28 A is 32.2 A — so a 30 A general-use switch is too small, even though 30 A sits above the running current. Combined with 430.102 (within sight) and 430.109 (permitted types), this completes the disconnect picture.
sections.on_the_job: Check two markings on a motor disconnect: the amp rating against 115 percent of table FLC, or the horsepower rating against the motor. If either fails, the disconnect is the wrong device even if it has worked for years on the old motor. On a Sharma commercial service call, a replacement 5 hp exhaust motor went in where the existing disconnect was a 30 A general-use switch. Table FLC is 28 A, so 430.110 wants at least 32.2 A — the 30 A switch came out and a 60 A switch went in, even though the old switch had 'always worked.'
sections.why_it_exists: A motor disconnect does not just carry current — it has to close onto a starting motor and open a running one without welding its contacts or failing in the switchman's hand. The 115 percent margin puts the switch's rating above the motor's full-load draw, so the device is never working at its limit every time the machine cycles.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is matching the disconnect to the breaker, or running the 115 percent off the nameplate amps. The breaker is sized from Table 430.52 percentages — a different rule. The disconnect starts from table full-load current under 430.6 and takes 115 percent, or it is picked by its horsepower rating. A 30 A switch 'because the motor draws 28' is the wrong answer.
inspection_fails: 30 A general-use switch disconnecting a motor that needs 32.2 A at 115 percent (430.110).
Disconnect picked to match the breaker, with no 115 percent or horsepower check.
Horsepower-rated switch smaller than the motor it disconnects.
Disconnect rating figured from nameplate FLA instead of table FLC (430.6, 430.110).

sections.title: Conductors to drives and power conversion equipment (430.122)
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 430.122 sizes the conductors feeding adjustable-speed drives and other power conversion equipment from the equipment's own ratings — not from the motor's horsepower table:
• Supply (input) conductors: ampacity not less than 125 percent of the drive's rated input current [430.122(A)]. The drive nameplate — input amps — is the document that sizes this wire.
• Output conductors, drive to motor: ampacity not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as determined by 430.6 [430.122(B)]. Where the drive is listed and marked "Suitable for Output Motor Conductor Protection," the output conductors must be at least the larger of that 125 percent value or the minimum conductor size marked on the drive.
• Where the equipment has a bypass, the section follows the larger demand — the conductors must suit the bypass arrangement as well as the drive [430.122(C)].
A drive can draw more at its input than the motor table suggests, so both sides of the drive get sized: input from the drive plate, output from the motor.
sections.on_the_job: Swapping a starter for a VFD on a pump or air handler: photograph the drive's input rating before ordering wire. Example: the plate reads INPUT 460 V, 21 A — the supply conductors need an ampacity of at least 21 × 1.25 = 26.25 A, whatever the motor table says. Reusing the old starter's wire size without the input-current check is the standard failure. Check the output side too: drive-to-motor conductors are sized at 125 percent of the motor's full-load current from 430.6.
sections.figure_idea: Nameplate zoom: 'INPUT 460 V 21 A' feeding the 125 percent math line.
sections.why_it_exists: A drive is not a starter. Its input current includes the losses and the harmonic-rich draw of the conversion electronics, and it is set by the drive's rating, not by the motor behind it. Wire sized from the motor table can run hot feeding a drive whose motor is loafing — and a later swap to a larger drive frame on the same motor silently overloads wire that nobody re-checked.
inspection_fails: Drive supply conductors sized from the motor horsepower table instead of the drive's rated input current.
Old starter wire reused on a VFD retrofit with no input-current check.
Output conductors to the motor undersized — not 125 percent of the motor full-load current.
Bypass installed and the conductors never checked for the across-the-line demand.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the drive's supply conductors from the motor's table full-load current (430.6, 430.22) because "it is a motor circuit." Part X changes the input side: supply conductors come from the drive's rated input current at 125 percent [430.122(A)]. The motor table still governs the output side — not the input.

rows: 125% of the drive rated input current, from the drive nameplate

figures.alt: Two-lane diagram of a drive installation: supply conductors sized at 125 percent of the drive rated input current (nameplate INPUT 460 V, 21 A, giving a 26.25 A minimum ampacity) feed the drive, and output conductors sized at 125 percent of motor full-load current per 430.6 run to the motor, with a bypass note and a fail strip against sizing the input from the motor horsepower table.

sections.title: Motor full-load current tables — the working values (430.248 / 430.250)
sections.plain_explanation:
Tables 430.248 (single-phase) and 430.250 (three-phase) give the table full-load current used for conductor, disconnect, controller, and short-circuit and ground-fault sizing under 430.6. The combinations in the tables on this page are the ones Sharma's crews meet most; the printed tables govern for anything not listed here.
• Read the value for the horsepower and for the voltage actually supplied — the same motor draws roughly half the current at the higher voltage.
• Use the table FLC even when the installed motor's nameplate amps differ. A replacement motor of the same horsepower uses the same table FLC.
• The nameplate is not ignored: it sets the overload protection (430.32). Table for sizing, nameplate for overloads — that split is 430.6.
sections.on_the_job: Keep the two bases separate (430.6): these table numbers size the wire, the disconnect, and the fault protection; the overloads still come off the nameplate of the motor actually installed. A replacement motor of the same horsepower uses the same table FLC even when its nameplate amps differ from the old motor's. Field example: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase well pump on a Marion County job — the table says 28 A, so the conductors size at 125 percent, 35 A, before anyone looks at the pump's nameplate; the overload setting still comes off that nameplate.
sections.figure_idea: Worksheet card: horsepower down the left, 115 / 208 / 230 / 460 V columns across, the common FLC values filled in — a glovebox version of Tables 430.248 and 430.250.
sections.why_it_exists: Motors of the same horsepower do not all draw the same current, and nameplates get swapped, painted over, and misread. The tables give every installer and inspector one standard current for a given horsepower and voltage, so the wire, disconnect, and fault protection come out the same on every job.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing the conductors from the nameplate amps because 'that is the real motor.' Under 430.6, conductors, disconnects, controllers, and fault protection are sized from the table FLC; the nameplate current is used for the overloads only. A motor with a low nameplate reading does not shrink the wire.
inspection_fails: Conductors sized from the nameplate amps instead of the Table 430.248/430.250 FLC (430.6).
Overload device set from the table value instead of the installed motor's nameplate (430.32).
230 V column used for a motor reconnected and running at 115 V — wrong FLC, wrong protection.
Replacement motor wired to the old motor's table value after a horsepower change.

sections.title: Air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment — article intro
sections.plain_explanation:
Article 440 takes hermetic refrigerant motor-compressors and air-conditioning equipment out of the general motor rules and gives them a nameplate-driven system.
• The equipment nameplate states the minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and the maximum overcurrent protection (MOCP, sometimes marked MOP or 'max fuse/breaker'), and those two printed numbers — not a horsepower table — size the circuit.
• Article 440 also sets the disconnect rule Sharma's crews use daily: within sight, readily accessible, at the equipment.
• Where 430 and 440 disagree for a compressor, 440 governs.
Florida settles the common condenser question for houses: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment on one- and two-family dwellings.
sections.on_the_job: Read the nameplate before you run the wire, every unit, every change-out. A replacement condenser with a higher MCA than the old one is a new circuit calculation, not a like-for-like swap. The arithmetic behind a typical plate: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current gives an MCA of 25 A (125 percent, per 440.32) and an MOCP of 35 A (175 percent, per 440.22(A)) — conductors at least the MCA, breaker never above the MOCP. Photograph the nameplate for the job file at rough-in and again at start-up.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice (tip, not an S-rule): the condenser is wired to the nameplate MOCP with a standard 2-pole breaker. The 210.8(F) GFCI question for outdoor outlets/equipment has varied by TIA and local amendment — confirm the AHJ position on the job rather than assuming; see the Chapter 2 cross-link on the 440.4(B) page.

nec2023_change.change: If unqualified people can readily reach an A/C or refrigeration disconnect, any door or hinged cover that exposes energized parts must take a tool to open or accept a lock. Disconnect readily accessible to unqualified people? A door or hinged cover that opens onto energized parts must need a tool or be lockable.

nec2023_change.source: Electrical Exam Coach, 2023 NEC change summary: 440.8 A/C equipment near tubs and showers

sections.why_it_exists: A hermetic compressor is sealed in a can with its overload protection inside it, and its starting current dwarfs its running current. General motor rules built on horsepower tables would mis-size both the wire and the breaker. The nameplate system puts the manufacturer's tested numbers in charge — MCA for the conductors, MOCP for the breaker — so the circuit matches the machine that actually shows up on the pad.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is sizing a condenser circuit from the tonnage or a horsepower table, or choosing the breaker to match the wire's ampacity. Article 440 is nameplate-driven: the MCA sizes the conductors and the MOCP caps the breaker, and the breaker is allowed to be larger than the conductor ampacity because the equipment's own overload protection does the running protection. Borrowing that allowance for a general circuit outside Article 440 is the second trap — it exists only inside this system.

sections.title: Reading the HVAC nameplate — MCA and MOCP do the sizing
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.4(B) covers the nameplate marking for equipment with a hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor. The plate carries the rated-load current and the branch-circuit selection current, and the manufacturer's marked minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and maximum overcurrent device rating (MOCP) are built from them. In field language:
• MCA tells you the smallest conductor ampacity the circuit may have.
• MOCP tells you the largest fuse or breaker you may protect it with.
A breaker smaller than MOCP is allowed; a conductor smaller than MCA is not. The plate, not a tonnage rule of thumb, is the calculation.
sections.on_the_job:
On every condenser and air handler: record MCA, MOCP, voltage, and phase from the plate. Wire to at least MCA, protect at no more than MOCP, and if the installed breaker or wire disagrees with a change-out unit's new plate, stop and tell the office before start-up — that is a change order conversation, not a field improvisation.

Worked example: a condenser plate reads MCA 24.5 A, MOCP 40 A. The conductor ampacity must be at least 24.5 A — 10 AWG copper (35 A at the 75°C column) covers it — and the breaker may be anything up to 40 A; Sharma's standard install protects it at the MOCP with a standard 2-pole breaker. A same-tonnage change-out plate reading MCA 17.5 / MOCP 30 is a different circuit — the plate, not the tons, decides.
sections.sharma_note: Cross-link (Chapter 2): the question of GFCI protection for outdoor HVAC equipment under 210.8(F) is handled on the Chapter 2 pages and is deliberately not resolved here; local AHJ position governs on the job.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: A hermetic compressor hides its motor inside the refrigerant circuit, so nobody can read a motor nameplate or apply the general motor tables to it. The manufacturer tests the whole unit and prints the answer: MCA already carries the 125 percent conductor sizing of 440.32, and MOCP already carries the starting-current allowance of 440.22. Reading the plate replaces a calculation the field cannot do — and removes the excuse for guessing from tonnage.
inspection_fails: Breaker larger than the nameplate MOCP left in place on a change-out — the old 50 A breaker kept for a unit marked MOCP 40.
Conductors below the plate MCA because 'it is only a 3-ton' — tonnage is not an ampacity.
New unit wired and started without anyone recording MCA and MOCP from the new plate.
Breaker swapped to a larger size to stop start-up trips instead of diagnosing the unit.
sections.exam_trap: The trap treats MCA and MOCP like a general-purpose circuit: 'MCA 24.5 A, so a 25 A breaker and wire sized to the breaker.' Two errors stack up. The conductor is sized to MCA, not to the breaker — and the breaker may be anything up to MOCP, here 40 A, larger than the conductor's plain ampacity, because the unit's own overload protection does the running protection. The mirror-image error — a breaker above MOCP 'because it trips' — is just as wrong.

figures.alt: A condenser nameplate marked MCA 24.5 A and MOCP 40 A, with the wire check — 10 AWG copper at 35 A covers the MCA — and the breaker check — 40 A at the MOCP, never above.
figures.caption: MCA is the wire floor; MOCP is the breaker ceiling.

page_quiz.question: A condenser plate reads MCA 24.5 A, MOCP 40 A. Which install complies?
choices: 10 AWG copper conductors and a 40 A breaker
12 AWG copper conductors and a 25 A breaker
10 AWG copper conductors and a 50 A breaker
Conductors sized to the tonnage, breaker at 40 A
page_quiz.explain_plain: 10 AWG copper at the 75 °C column is 35 A — at or above the 24.5 A MCA — and 40 A is at, not above, the MOCP. 12 AWG falls below MCA, and 50 A exceeds MOCP.

page_quiz.question: Which statement about MCA and MOCP is right?
choices: The breaker must equal the MCA
A breaker smaller than MOCP is allowed; a conductor smaller than MCA is not
The conductor may be smaller than MCA if the breaker is small
MOCP is the minimum breaker size
page_quiz.explain_plain: MCA is a floor for the conductor; MOCP is a ceiling for the protective device. Anything at or below the ceiling protects the circuit.

page_quiz.question: On a change-out, the new unit is the same tonnage but its plate reads MCA 17.5 / MOCP 30, and the existing circuit is heavier. What decides the install?
choices: The tonnage — same size, same circuit
The existing breaker, since it passed before
page_quiz.explain_plain: The plate, not the tons, is the calculation. A different plate is a different circuit; a mismatch with the installed breaker or wire is a change-order conversation before start-up.

sections.title: Short-circuit current rating of air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.10 requires the motor controllers, the disconnecting means, and the combination load controllers used with air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to have a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) at least equal to the available fault current where the equipment is installed. The rating is marked on the equipment. It is the Article 440 companion to 408.6 for panelboards and 409.110 for industrial control panels.
• MCA and MOCP can both be perfect and the installation can still be wrong: a unit whose SCCR sits below the available fault current is a mismatch.
• The SCCR is read off the unit nameplate or control panel label, with the MCA and MOCP, before the unit is set.
• The available fault current comes from the utility or the design documents. It is never estimated in the field.
The problem arises on commercial rooftops and larger services, where fault current runs high. It rarely decides anything on a house condenser.
sections.on_the_job:
On commercial HVAC work, add SCCR to the nameplate photograph set: MCA, MOCP, and SCCR, plus the available fault current when the design provides it. A mismatch goes to Mike before the unit is set, not to the inspector at final.
Worked case, a rooftop package unit on a small retail job: the design shows 22 kA of available fault current. The first unit submitted is marked SCCR 10 kA — it cannot be installed, even though its MCA and MOCP fit the circuit. The approved unit is marked 65 kA, which covers the 22 kA. Record both numbers, the marked SCCR and the available fault current, in the job file.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: Fault current is what the service can push into a dead short. Gear built for less than that does not clear the fault — it becomes the fault: contacts weld, enclosures rupture, and the failure happens in front of whoever is standing at the unit. The SCCR marking exists so the comparison is made on paper, from the nameplate and the design, before the equipment is set.
inspection_fails: Packaged unit installed where the available fault current exceeds its marked SCCR.
No SCCR comparison on record — the submittal shows MCA and MOCP only.
Control panel label missing or illegible, so the SCCR cannot be verified.
Change-out unit set with a lower SCCR than the equipment it replaced, never re-checked against the service.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is treating SCCR as one more number the nameplate sizes for you, like MCA or MOCP. Those two size the circuit to the unit. SCCR runs the other way: the building's available fault current is fixed by the service, and the unit's marked rating has to cover it. A 10 kA unit on a 22 kA service fails even with perfect wire and the perfect breaker.

sections.title: Rating the air-conditioning disconnect (440.12)
sections.plain_explanation:
The disconnecting means for hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor equipment is rated under 440.12, separately from the branch-circuit protection in 440.22. The disconnect's ampere rating must be at least 115 percent of the nameplate rated-load current or the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater — or the disconnect may be chosen by the horsepower-equivalent method the section allows. A disconnect that matches the breaker size by habit can still be undersized by this section, because the two devices answer different questions.
• Rating: this page — 115 percent of the greater nameplate current (440.12).
• Location: within sight of the equipment (440.14).
• Protection: the breaker or fuses answer to 440.22 and the nameplate MOCP.
sections.on_the_job: Worked example: nameplate rated-load current 28 A. Disconnect minimum: 28 × 1.15 = 32.2 A — so the common 60 A disconnect is the shelf pick, and a 30 A disconnect fails this section even though it exceeds the running amps. Sharma practice at trim: the condenser gets a standard disconnect and whip, set within sight of the unit (440.14) — and the rating still comes from this section, while the breaker follows the nameplate MOCP under 440.22. When a change-out unit's plate shows a higher rated-load current than the old one, re-run the 115 percent before reusing the old disconnect.
sections.sharma_note: Sharma practice (not code): the condenser gets a standard disconnect and whip at trim — the rating still comes from this section, and the breaker follows the nameplate under S-03.
sections.figure_idea: Disconnect rating card: RLA × 1.15 arrow to the next standard disconnect size.
sections.edition_note:
No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed.
FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.
sections.why_it_exists: The disconnect is the switch the service tech throws and then trusts with his hands inside the unit. It carries the compressor's current through every start, all day, for years — so it is rated above the running current, not at it. An undersized disconnect overheats at its contacts, welds, or burns open, and the 'off' the tech trusted is not off at all.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'The disconnect matches the 30 A breaker, so it must be right.' With a 28 A rated-load current, the disconnect minimum is 32.2 A — the matched pair is a violation. The breaker answers to 440.22 and the nameplate MOCP; the disconnect answers to 440.12 at 115 percent. Different questions, different numbers.
inspection_fails: 30 A disconnect on a unit with 28 A rated-load current — under the 115 percent minimum (440.12).
Disconnect rating copied from the breaker size instead of the nameplate current (440.12).
Fused disconnect fitted with fuses above the nameplate MOCP (440.22).
Disconnect mounted out of sight of the condenser (440.14).

tables.caption: Rating the disconnect — worked ratings (440.12)
tables.note: Or use the horsepower-equivalent method 440.12 allows. The branch-circuit breaker is sized separately under 440.22 and the nameplate MOCP.

page_quiz.question: Nameplate rated-load current is 28 A. Smallest permitted disconnect rating?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 28 × 1.15 = 32.2 A (440.12) — which is why the standard 60 A disconnect is the shelf pick and a 30 A fails.

page_quiz.question: The disconnect rating under 440.12 is based on:
choices: 115% of the nameplate rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater
page_quiz.explain_plain: 440.12 rates the disconnect at not less than 115 percent of the greater of the two nameplate currents.

page_quiz.question: Which device provides the branch-circuit short-circuit protection for the same unit?
choices: The breaker or fuses sized under 440.22 / nameplate MOCP
The disconnect only if it is fusible
page_quiz.explain_plain: Branch-circuit protection is 440.22's job, worked to the marked MOCP; the disconnect is rated under 440.12 for service duty, not protection.

sections.title: The HVAC disconnect — within sight and readily accessible
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.14 requires the disconnecting means for air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to be within sight from the equipment and readily accessible to it, with an exception for certain industrial/process installations where conditions are met.
• 'Within sight' carries the Article 100 meaning: visible and within 50 ft.
• The disconnect may be on the equipment or separate from it, but a person servicing the unit must be able to reach it and see the unit from it.
• A breaker inside the house panel does not satisfy this by itself.
• The disconnect also may not be mounted on a panel that is designed to allow access to the equipment itself, and it may not be placed where it obscures the equipment nameplate.
sections.on_the_job: Set the disconnect where the service tech stands: at the condenser pad, in sight, with working space in front of it, not behind a fence line or above reach. On a Marion Oaks change-out, the old disconnect sat in the old unit's shadow, so we relocated it onto the wall 8 ft from the new condenser as part of the job and noted it on the invoice record. Measure the sight line, not just the distance: at 8 ft the tech sees the unit and the disconnect in one look. If the old disconnect was never installed, add it — the change-out is not finished without it.
sections.florida_note: Florida note: exterior disconnects live in weather — use listed outdoor equipment and keep the working space clear of the condensate line and landscaping at final.

nec2023_change.change: The A/C and refrigeration disconnect now has to have 110.26(A) working space, on top of the long-standing in-sight and readily accessible rules. The disconnect for A/C or refrigeration equipment must now have working space that meets 110.26(A).

sections.why_it_exists: A tech working on a condenser has the cabinet open and his hands inside. If the only way to kill power is a breaker inside the house, someone can flip it back on without knowing he is there, and he cannot lock it out from where he stands. A disconnect he can see and reach means the unit stays dead while he works, and he can prove it is dead before he touches anything.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer is that the breaker in the house panel is the disconnect. It is not: 440.14 wants a disconnect within sight of the equipment — visible and not over 50 ft away — and readily accessible to it. A second trap is reading 'within sight' as 'on the same lot'; a disconnect 80 ft away around the corner fails both parts of the test.
inspection_fails: No disconnect at the condenser at all — only the breaker inside the house panel.
Disconnect mounted on the unit's own access panel, so it comes off with the panel.
Disconnect set where it covers the equipment nameplate.
Disconnect behind a fence or above reach — not readily accessible from the unit.
Disconnect out of view of the unit, even though it is under 50 ft away.

rows: On or near the equipment — not on its access panel
Readily accessible — reach it without climbing
Stays readable — never mount over it

choices: Visible from the equipment and within 50 ft
page_quiz.explain_plain: Within sight is the Article 100 term: visible, and not more than 50 ft away.

Yes, if the breaker is lockable
No — the disconnect must be within sight of and readily accessible to the equipment
No — the disconnect must be inside the unit
page_quiz.explain_plain: A breaker inside the house is neither visible from the unit nor reachable by the tech standing at it.

page_quiz.question: Where may the 440.14 disconnect NOT be mounted?
choices: On the wall beside the unit
On a panel designed to allow access to the equipment
On a post at the pad
page_quiz.explain_plain: The disconnect cannot ride on the equipment's access panel, and it cannot cover the nameplate.

sections.title: Short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a compressor circuit
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.22 sizes the branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a hermetic motor-compressor circuit. It ties the device to the equipment's rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater; on a listed unit, the marked MOCP on the nameplate is the number the installer works to. As with motors generally, this device is allowed to be larger than the conductor's plain ampacity, because the equipment's own overload protection does the running protection and the breaker must ride through compressor starting current. That allowance only exists inside Article 440's system — never borrow it for a general circuit.
• The arithmetic behind the nameplate MOCP, from 440.22(A): not more than 175 percent of the rated-load or branch-circuit selection current.
• If a device at 175 percent will not carry the starting current, the rating may be increased, but not above 225 percent.
• 440.22(A) also sets a floor: the device may not be less than 125 percent of the rated-load current.
• Worked example: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current takes protection at 20 × 1.75 = 35 A; if 35 A will not start it, the ceiling is 20 × 2.25 = 45 A. On listed equipment the manufacturer's printed MOCP already reflects this math, so the plate still governs — this arithmetic is for the compressor-only case and for checking a plate that looks wrong.
• 440.22(B) covers equipment with more than one motor or other loads.
sections.on_the_job: If a condenser trips a breaker sized at or below its MOCP, the fault is in the equipment or the circuit, not in the arithmetic: measure starting and running current and inspect the contactor and conductors before anyone proposes a larger breaker. A breaker above the nameplate MOCP is never the fix. On a Sharma change-out, the new unit's plate is photographed at set time, and the existing breaker is checked against the new MOCP before the disconnect is closed.
sections.why_it_exists: A hermetic compressor starts hard, and its motor is sealed inside the shell under the equipment's own overload protection. The branch device has one job: clear a short circuit or ground fault without tripping on every start. Sizing it by house-circuit rules would nuisance-trip a healthy unit; oversizing it past the MOCP leaves fault energy unchecked.
sections.exam_trap: The trap is reaching for a bigger breaker when a condenser trips — 'go up one size and see.' If the breaker is already at the nameplate MOCP, a larger one violates 440.22 and hides the real fault. The other trap pick: sizing the device at 175% of the MCA. The percentages run off rated-load or branch-circuit selection current, not MCA.
inspection_fails: Breaker larger than the nameplate MOCP on a listed condenser (440.22).
Device below 125% of rated-load current, tripping on every compressor start (440.22(A)).
Protection raised past 225% of rated-load current because the unit 'would not start.'
Article 440 percentages borrowed for a general-purpose circuit outside Article 440.

tables.caption: 440.22(A) — the three numbers
rows: Ceiling — only if 175% won't start it
tables.note: On listed equipment, work to the nameplate MOCP; this arithmetic checks the plate or covers the compressor-only case.

figures.alt: Scale bar from 0 to 50 amperes for a compressor with a 20 ampere rated-load current: below 25 amperes is under the 125 percent floor, 25 to 35 amperes is the normal window, 35 to 45 amperes is allowed only if 175 percent will not start the compressor, and over 45 amperes passes the 225 percent ceiling.
figures.caption: The MOCP window: floor at 125%, standard maximum at 175%, hard ceiling at 225%.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 175% of rated-load current: 20 × 1.75 = 35 A.

page_quiz.explain_plain: 440.22(A) allows an increase only where 175% will not carry the starting current, and never above 225%.

page_quiz.question: On a listed condensing unit, which number does the installer work to?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The manufacturer's printed MOCP already reflects the 440.22(A) math; the plate governs on listed equipment.

sections.title: Conductor sizing for a single motor-compressor
sections.plain_explanation:
Section 440.32 sizes conductors for a single hermetic motor-compressor:
• The conductor ampacity must be not less than 125 percent of the compressor's rated-load current, or of the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater.
• On listed equipment the manufacturer has already done this work and printed it as the MCA (minimum circuit ampacity) on the nameplate. The field rule and the nameplate rule agree: the conductor ampacity must be at least the MCA.
• Where you are sizing from a compressor's own data rather than a unit plate — a compressor-only replacement — this section is the arithmetic behind the plate.
Worked example: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current needs conductors with an ampacity of at least 20 × 1.25 = 25 A, before any other checks.
sections.on_the_job: When the plate is present, wire to the MCA and do not re-derive it — on a condenser change-out, the MCA and MOCP printed on the new unit's plate are the whole sizing job. When the plate is missing or illegible on existing equipment, stop and get the data from the manufacturer rather than estimating from tonnage: a "3-ton" guess is not a current rating, and two units of the same tonnage can carry different compressors. Photograph the plate at the survey so the wire gets ordered right the first time.
sections.why_it_exists: A compressor runs for hours at a stretch through a Florida summer, and its current does not politely stop at the nameplate value on a hot roof or a low-voltage afternoon. The 125 percent margin keeps the conductors from living at their temperature limit for the whole cooling season — which is what cooks insulation, loosens terminations and starts nuisance trips that turn into callbacks.
inspection_fails: Conductors sized to the MOCP, or to a tonnage guess, instead of the nameplate MCA.
Old conductors reused on a change-out without checking them against the new unit's MCA.
Compressor-only replacement wired from the old unit's plate instead of the new compressor's rated-load or selection current.
MCA guessed from a faded, sun-bleached plate — the data was never pulled from the manufacturer.
sections.exam_trap: The trap answer sizes the wire from the MOCP — or from tonnage. The MOCP is short-circuit and ground-fault protection (440.22), and it is allowed to be far larger than the conductor ampacity; it does not size the wire. Conductors come from the MCA, which is 440.32's 125 percent already worked out by the manufacturer.

tables.caption: The two plate numbers — do not swap them
rows: Conductors: ampacity at least the MCA (440.32, worked out)
Breaker or fuses: short-circuit protection only (440.22)

figures.alt: Flow diagram: a compressor nameplate rated-load current of 20 A multiplied by 125 percent under 440.32 gives a 25 A minimum conductor ampacity; on listed equipment that number is printed as the MCA, and a warning panel states the MOCP and tonnage do not size the wire.
figures.caption: RLC × 125% = minimum conductor ampacity. On a listed unit, that number is the MCA.

page_quiz.question: Conductors for a single motor-compressor are sized at not less than what percent of the rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater?
page_quiz.explain_plain: 440.32 sets the floor at 125 percent of the greater of rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current.

page_quiz.question: On listed equipment, which nameplate value is the minimum conductor ampacity?
page_quiz.explain_plain: The MCA is the manufacturer's worked-out 440.32 result; the conductor ampacity must be at least the MCA.

page_quiz.question: A compressor has a rated-load current of 20 A. From 440.32 alone, the minimum conductor ampacity is:
page_quiz.explain_plain: 20 A × 1.25 = 25 A minimum conductor ampacity.

sections.title: Room air conditioners (440.60–440.65)
sections.plain_explanation:
Part VII of Article 440 covers the cord-and-plug room air conditioner — the window and through-wall units a tenant or homeowner plugs in. Part VII covers room units rated not over 40 A, 250 V, single-phase (440.62(A)).
• A single room unit on a branch circuit of its own may not exceed 80 percent of that circuit's rating.
• Where the same circuit also feeds lighting or other receptacles, the unit may not exceed 50 percent of the circuit rating.
• 440.65 adds the plug protection: single-phase room units must have leakage-current detection (LCDI) or arc-fault protection in the attachment plug or cord.
• 440.65 also allows a factory-installed heat-detecting circuit interrupter (HDCI) besides LCDI or AFCI on single-phase cord-and-plug room air conditioners.
The fat plug with the test buttons is a requirement, not an accessory.
sections.on_the_job: A window unit tripping a shared bedroom circuit is usually the 50 percent rule announcing itself. The numbers: a 12 A unit in a Winter Garden rental bedroom sits on a 20 A circuit that also feeds the lights and receptacles, so the cap is 50 percent — 10 A — and the unit is already over it. The fix is a dedicated circuit under the 80 percent rule, where the cap is 16 A and the 12 A unit fits — not a bigger breaker on the shared circuit.
sections.figure_idea: Two bars: dedicated circuit — unit up to 80 percent; shared circuit — unit capped at 50 percent.
sections.why_it_exists: A room unit is a motor load that runs for hours, plugged into whatever circuit is nearby. On a shared circuit it can hold half the capacity all afternoon, heating wiring that was roughed for lights and chargers. The plug protection exists because these cords get pinched in windows, aged and wet; LCDI, AFCI or HDCI in the plug catches cord damage before it starts a fire.
sections.exam_trap: The trap: 'The unit draws 12 A and the breaker is 20 A, so it complies.' On a circuit shared with lighting or other receptacles the cap is 50 percent of the rating — 10 A on a 20 A circuit — so the 12 A unit fails. The 80 percent figure only applies when the unit is alone on its own branch circuit.
inspection_fails: 12 A window unit on a 20 A bedroom circuit shared with lighting — over the 50 percent cap of 10 A, 440.62.
Room unit's LCDI plug cut off and replaced with a plain plug after nuisance trips, 440.65.
'Dedicated circuit' fixed by swapping in a larger breaker on the shared circuit instead of running a new circuit.
Room unit rated 45 A treated under Part VII — Part VII stops at 40 A, 250 V, single-phase, 440.62(A).

tables.caption: Room unit caps by circuit (440.62)
tables.note: Part VII covers room units rated not over 40 A, 250 V, single-phase (440.62(A)).

figures.alt: Bar chart on a 20 A circuit showing a room air conditioner capped at 80 percent (16 A) on a dedicated circuit and at 50 percent (10 A) on a shared circuit, with an example 12 A unit line that fits the dedicated circuit and fails the shared one.
figures.caption: Same unit, same breaker — the circuit it shares decides the cap.

page_quiz.question: A room air conditioner alone on its own 20 A branch circuit may draw at most:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Dedicated circuit: the cap is 80 percent of 20 A = 16 A.

page_quiz.question: The same unit on a 20 A circuit that also feeds bedroom lighting may draw at most:
page_quiz.explain_plain: Shared circuit: the cap drops to 50 percent of 20 A = 10 A.

page_quiz.question: Single-phase room air conditioners must have which protection in the attachment plug or cord?
choices: LCDI or arc-fault protection (factory HDCI also permitted)
